section.title: Christianity: Practices
section.blurb: How Christians worship, pray, celebrate sacraments and festivals, and serve local and worldwide communities.

topics.title: Worship: liturgical, non-liturgical, informal and private
topics.overview: Worship is how Christians show love and respect for God. There are many forms, and exam questions often ask you to compare them.

bullets: To praise and thank God, to say sorry, to ask for help, and to grow closer to God.
Public worship also builds community and strengthens faith.
The early Christians met regularly for 'the apostles' teaching and fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer' (Acts 2:42). Christians are told not to give up meeting together (Hebrews 10:25).
Jesus promised 'where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am' (Matthew 18:20), so Christians believe God is present when they worship together.

**Liturgical worship** follows a set order and set words, such as the Catholic Mass, the Orthodox Divine Liturgy and Church of England services. Advantages: familiar, shared with Christians worldwide, and focuses on God through tradition.
**Non-liturgical worship** has a looser structure with hymns, Bible readings, prayers and a sermon, but no fixed words (many Baptist and Methodist churches). It emphasises the Bible and the sermon.
**Informal (charismatic) worship** is spontaneous and led by the Holy Spirit: modern music, clapping, raised hands, speaking in tongues and spontaneous prayer (Pentecostal churches).
**Informal (waiting) worship:** Quakers sit in silence with no leader until someone feels moved by the Spirit to speak.

**Liturgical:** the same words are used worldwide, so a Catholic can join Mass anywhere; set words help people who struggle to find their own; it links believers with centuries of tradition. Some find it can become routine.
**Non-liturgical:** the minister can choose readings and prayers to suit the congregation and current events; the sermon explaining the Bible is central. Some miss the sense of tradition.
**Informal / charismatic:** feels lively and personal, and believers feel the Holy Spirit is at work, which attracts many young people. Others find it noisy or too focused on feelings.
**Quaker silence:** allows everyone to listen for God without distraction and treats all as equal. Some find long silence difficult.
**Private:** can happen at any time, fits around daily life and builds a personal relationship with God. However, it lacks the support and fellowship of a community.
Most worship includes Bible readings, a sermon and hymns based on scripture. Catholics read set passages each week; many Protestants focus on the sermon explaining the Bible.
Christians use the Bible to learn about God and God's will (2 Timothy 3:16).
In Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican services, readings follow a **lectionary** (a set cycle of readings), and the Gospel is often carried in procession and read standing, to show its importance.
In many Protestant churches the **sermon** explaining a passage is the centre of the service; the pulpit may be placed in the middle of the church.
In private worship Christians may follow Bible-reading notes or a daily plan, or use 'lectio divina' (slow, prayerful reading of a short passage).
Worship alone or at home: prayer, reading the Bible, meditation or using aids like a rosary, icons or a cross.
Jesus taught that private prayer is valuable: 'go into your room, close the door and pray' (Matthew 6:6).
It allows a personal relationship with God at any time, away from stress.

views.label: Quakers

In 12-mark answers, do not just say a type of worship is 'more effective'. Give the reason (for example 'set words unite Christians worldwide').

topics.title: Prayer
topics.overview: Prayer is communicating with God. It is central to Christian life and worship, and the Lord's Prayer is the model.

bullets: Use the memory aid: sorry (confession), thank you (thanksgiving), please (asking for help for self or others), and praise (adoration).
It helps Christians build a relationship with God and listen to him.
It brings peace, strength in hard times and helps them accept God's will.
A common pattern is **ACTS**: Adoration (praise), Confession (saying sorry), Thanksgiving and Supplication (asking for themselves or others; prayer for others is called **intercession**).
Jesus himself prayed alone, for example early in the morning in a deserted place (Mark 1:35), so Christians follow his example.

notes.h: The words of the Lord's Prayer (modern version)
bullets: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread. Forgive us our sins as we forgive those who sin against us.
Lead us not into temptation but deliver us from evil. For the kingdom, the power and the glory are yours, now and for ever. Amen.
The final line (the 'doxology') was added by the early Church; Catholics say it separately during Mass.
**Set prayers** are written and used by many people, such as the Lord's Prayer and the Hail Mary. They are familiar, link Christians together and help those who struggle to find words.
**Informal prayers** are spontaneous and in your own words. They feel personal and honest and can be said anywhere.
Prayer may be silent, spoken, sung or involve actions such as kneeling or the sign of the cross.
Some Christians use aids such as rosary beads (Catholic), icons and the Jesus Prayer (Orthodox), or a prayer journal.

Some Protestants warn against set prayers becoming 'vain repetitions' (Matthew 6:7) said without thinking, so they prefer informal prayer. Others reply that set prayers like the Lord's Prayer were given by Jesus himself.
Jesus taught this prayer to his disciples (Matthew 6:9-13; Luke 11:2-4).
It praises God ('hallowed be your name'), asks for God's kingdom and for daily needs ('give us today our daily bread'), asks for forgiveness and asks for protection from temptation.
It teaches Christians to forgive others as God forgives them.
It is used in almost all worship, including Holy Communion, baptism, weddings and funerals, and in many schools.

Explain why prayer is significant (relationship with God, strength, forgiveness), not just what happens.

topics.title: The sacraments: baptism
topics.overview: Sacraments are special rituals that bring Christians closer to God. Baptism is the sacrament of welcome into the Church, and Christians disagree about infant and believers' baptism.

bullets: St Augustine described a sacrament as 'an outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace'.
Catholic and Orthodox Christians have seven sacraments: baptism, confirmation, Eucharist, reconciliation (confession), anointing of the sick, marriage and ordination.
Most Protestants (e.g. Church of England, Methodists) recognise two: baptism and Holy Communion. The Salvation Army and Quakers have none.
Baptism is using water to show cleansing from sin, new life with Jesus and becoming part of the Church.
Jesus was baptised by John (Mark 1:9-11) and told his disciples to baptise (Matthew 28:19).
It symbolises dying to sin and rising to new life; in many churches the Holy Spirit is received.
**Purposes** of baptism (often asked): to wash away sin, to join the Church, to follow Jesus' example and command, to receive the Holy Spirit and God's grace, and to begin a new life as a Christian.
Jesus said 'unless one is born of water and spirit, he can't enter into God's Kingdom' (John 3:5).

**Infant (Church of England or Catholic):** at the **font**, the priest makes the sign of the cross on the baby's forehead, pours water three times in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, may anoint with oil, gives a lit candle (passing from darkness to light) and, in Catholic practice, a white garment (new life and purity). Parents and godparents reject evil and promise to raise the child as a Christian.

**Believers' (Baptist):** the person gives a **testimony** (how they came to faith), then goes down into a pool called a **baptistery** or into a river or the sea and is fully immersed. Going under the water symbolises dying to the old life; coming up symbolises rising to new life with Christ (Romans 6:4).
Anglicans and Catholics later have **confirmation**, when a young person confirms for themselves the promises made at their baptism.
Practised by Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans and Methodists.
Water is poured or sprinkled (Orthodox infants are immersed) in the name of the Trinity. Parents and godparents promise to bring the child up in the faith.
Reasons: Catholics believe it removes original sin; it welcomes the child into the Church; parents thank God; Jesus welcomed children (Mark 10:14).
Practised by Baptists and Pentecostals. Only people old enough to understand and choose faith are baptised.
The person is fully immersed in a pool or river, often after giving a testimony (their story of faith).
Reasons: faith must be a personal choice, and the New Testament shows believers baptised after repenting (Acts 2:38).
For: removes original sin, joins the child to the Church, follows household baptisms in the New Testament.
Against: babies cannot choose faith, and baptism should follow belief.
For: the New Testament records whole households being baptised (Acts 16:33), which may have included children; baptism is a gift of God's grace, not a reward for understanding.
Against: in the New Testament baptism follows repentance and faith (Acts 2:38; the Ethiopian official in Acts 8:36-38); Jesus himself was baptised as an adult.

Many churches that baptise infants also offer adult baptism to people who become Christians later, and some churches that practise believers' baptism hold a **service of dedication** or thanksgiving for babies instead.

views.label: Baptist/Pentecostal

topics.title: The sacraments: Holy Communion and how it is celebrated
topics.overview: Holy Communion (Eucharist, Mass, Lord's Supper) remembers Jesus' Last Supper. Christians disagree about what happens to the bread and wine and about how to celebrate it.

bullets: At the Last Supper Jesus broke bread and shared wine, saying 'this is my body... this is my blood' and 'do this in remembrance of me' (Matthew 26:26-28; Luke 22:19).
Christians receive bread and wine to remember Jesus' sacrifice, thank God, receive grace and strengthen faith.
It unites the congregation and encourages Christians to serve others and work for justice (the community and wider society).

Different names show different emphases: **Eucharist** (thanksgiving), **Mass** (Catholic), **Holy Communion** (sharing with God and each other), **the Lord's Supper** or **Breaking of Bread** (many Protestants), **Divine Liturgy** (the Orthodox service).
Paul says 'there is one loaf of bread, we, who are many, are one body' (1 Corinthians 10:17), so Communion shows the unity of believers.

For the community: it brings the parish together, and many churches link it with action, such as collecting food for food banks or praying for those in need. For society: it reminds Christians that Jesus' body was 'given for you', inspiring self-giving service.
**Catholics:** transubstantiation. The bread and wine become the body and blood of Jesus while still looking the same. Jesus is really present (John 6:53-54).
**Orthodox:** they believe in the real presence of Christ as a holy mystery, without explaining how.
**Church of England:** varies: some believe in a real or spiritual presence, others see it as a memorial.
**Many Protestants (Baptist, Methodist, others):** a symbolic memorial of the Last Supper, remembering Jesus' sacrifice.
**Lutherans:** Christ is truly present 'in, with and under' the bread and wine, which remain bread and wine. This is sometimes called consubstantiation (a term Lutherans themselves rarely use).
**Catholic Mass:** Liturgy of the Word, then bread (wafer) and wine are consecrated by the priest. Congregation says responses and the Creed; shares the sign of peace.
**Orthodox Divine Liturgy:** held in front of and behind the iconostasis (screen of icons). Communion is given on a spoon, with bread and wine mixed in the chalice. Children are included.
**Methodist (and many Protestants):** hymns, Bible reading and sermon, then the minister repeats Jesus' words. An 'open table' welcomes all baptised Christians. Non-alcoholic wine in small cups.
**Quakers and Salvation Army** do not celebrate it as a sacrament.

views.label: Church of England

topics.title: Pilgrimage: Lourdes and Iona
topics.overview: A pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place for religious reasons. The AQA spec requires two contrasting examples: Lourdes and Iona.

bullets: To grow closer to God, strengthen faith, pray, seek forgiveness or healing, and reflect on life.
To meet other Christians and to step away from everyday life.
A pilgrimage is both a physical journey and a spiritual one.
Pilgrimage is not compulsory for Christians (unlike Hajj in Islam). It is a personal choice to deepen faith.
Some go to help others: many volunteers take sick and disabled pilgrims to Lourdes and care for them there.
Jesus' family went to Jerusalem every year for Passover (Luke 2:41), so pilgrimage has roots in the Bible.
In 1858 a girl called Bernadette Soubirous said the Virgin Mary appeared to her 18 times in a cave (the Grotto). Mary told her to dig, and a spring appeared, now believed by many to heal.
It is a Catholic pilgrimage site visited by millions each year, and many sick and disabled pilgrims go hoping for healing or comfort.
Activities: bathing in the spring water, drinking it, praying at the Grotto, the torchlight procession with the Rosary, Mass at the Basilica and the Stations of the Cross. Volunteers help the sick.
Importance: it is a place of healing, prayer and sharing faith; many report spiritual peace even if not physically cured.

The Catholic Church has officially recognised 72 healings at Lourdes as miracles (the 72nd was announced in 2025), after checks by doctors at the Lourdes Medical Bureau. Thousands more claim healing that has not been officially confirmed.
A small island off Scotland where St Columba founded a monastery in 563 AD, spreading Christianity in Scotland and beyond.
The Iona Community (founded in 1938 by George MacLeod) is an ecumenical community working for peace and justice. Pilgrims stay at the abbey and centres.
Activities: daily worship in the abbey, walking the island, quiet prayer and reflection, Bible study and workshops.
Importance: a peaceful, simple place that helps pilgrims reflect and connect with Celtic Christian tradition.
Lourdes: Catholic, focused on Mary, healing and the sick, busy with large crowds.
Iona: ecumenical (all denominations), quiet, reflective, focused on community and justice, with a small number of visitors.

Other pilgrimages: Jerusalem and the Holy Land (where Jesus lived, died and rose), Rome, Canterbury, Walsingham in Norfolk (a shrine to Mary for Catholics and Anglicans), Holy Island (Lindisfarne) and Santiago de Compostela.

views.text: Pilgrimage, especially to sites linked with Mary and saints, is a way of seeking grace, healing and forgiveness.

views.label: Many Protestants
views.text: Pilgrimage is optional and not essential; what matters is faith, though sites like Iona are valued for reflection.

views.label: Quaker
views.text: No place is holier than another, because God can be met anywhere; an outward journey is not needed for an inner one.

topics.title: Celebrating festivals: Christmas and Easter
topics.overview: Christmas and Easter are the two main Christian festivals. They celebrate the incarnation and the resurrection, and they matter to Christians in Great Britain today.

bullets: Celebrates the birth of Jesus: the incarnation, when God became human.

Practices: Advent (preparing), nativity plays and cribs, carol services, Midnight Mass or Christmas Day services, lights and decorations (Jesus is the light of the world), giving gifts (like the wise men) and giving to charity.
Importance in Great Britain today: many people celebrate it as a holiday, so Christians stress the religious meaning. Churches run services, community meals and charity work, e.g. for the homeless.
Midnight Mass on Christmas Eve, Christingle services (an orange with a candle representing Jesus the light of the world), and the Nativity story read from Matthew and Luke.
Many churches hold their best-attended services of the year at Christmas, including people who rarely attend church.
**Palm Sunday:** Jesus' entry into Jerusalem; palm crosses are given out.
**Maundy Thursday:** the Last Supper and Jesus washing the disciples' feet; Communion and foot-washing services.
**Good Friday:** Jesus' crucifixion; churches are bare, Stations of the Cross, solemn services, hot cross buns.
**Easter Day:** Jesus' resurrection; joyful services, flowers, 'Christ is risen' / 'He is risen indeed', Easter vigil with the Paschal candle, Easter eggs as symbols of new life.
**Lent:** 40 days of fasting and prayer before Easter.
**Ash Wednesday** begins Lent: Catholics and Anglicans receive a cross of ash on the forehead as a sign of repentance.
Easter has no fixed date: it falls on the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the spring equinox, so between 22 March and 25 April (Western churches). Orthodox Easter is often later.
Easter is the most important festival because it celebrates the resurrection, the basis of Christian faith.
Both are public holidays. Many non-religious people celebrate them too, so Christians may worry about commercialisation but also see opportunities to share their faith.
They bring church communities together and inspire charity (Christmas) and hope (Easter).
Christmas and Easter shape the British calendar: school holidays and bank holidays (Christmas Day, Boxing Day, Good Friday, Easter Monday in England and Wales).
The King's Christmas broadcast often speaks about the Christian meaning of Christmas, and the King gives Maundy money to older people on Maundy Thursday.
Christians may see the festivals as a chance for mission (carol services, Easter events) and charity (Christmas meals for the homeless, Christian Aid and Crisis appeals).

topics.title: The role of the Church in the local community: food banks
topics.overview: Churches serve their local communities in many practical ways. Food banks are a key AQA example of Christians helping people in need.

notes.h: The Church in the local community
bullets: A local church provides worship, baptisms, weddings and funerals, pastoral care and Bible study.
It also runs youth groups, toddler groups, luncheon clubs, schools and community halls, and supports those in need.
The Church (all Christians) campaigns for justice and runs charities.

Other examples: coffee mornings and lunch clubs for lonely or elderly people, parent and toddler groups, debt advice (for example Christians Against Poverty), night shelters, community meals, and opening the building as a quiet place to pray or a warm space in winter.
Churches also hold services for local events, such as Remembrance Sunday or memorials after a tragedy.

Food banks give emergency food parcels to people who cannot afford food. The **Trussell Trust**, a charity founded on Christian principles, runs the UK's largest network. In 2025 food banks in its network gave out about 2.6 million emergency parcels, around 900,000 of them for children, from about 1,700 locations (Trussell figures published 2026). Many are based in churches and run by volunteers.
People are usually referred by professionals such as doctors or social workers and receive a voucher for a parcel. Food is donated by churches, schools and supermarkets.
Many churches also offer a friendly welcome, advice and a listening ear to those who come.
Other examples: the Oasis Project (Plymouth Methodists) runs training, job clubs and food support.
Jesus taught that helping the hungry is helping him (Matthew 25:35-40).
The Golden Rule and 'love your neighbour' (Mark 12:31) encourage practical help.
James says faith without action is dead (James 2:17).
The Parable of the Good Samaritan teaches helping anyone in need.

views.label: All Christians
views.text: Agree that caring for the poor is a duty, but some focus on charity (food banks) while others also campaign for political change so fewer people need food banks.

topics.title: The role of the Church in the local community: Street Pastors
topics.overview: Street Pastors are trained Christian volunteers who care for people on the streets at night. They show Christian love in action.

bullets: A Christian charity started in Brixton, London, in 2003 by Rev. Les Isaac and colleagues from the Ascension Trust.
Trained volunteers from local churches patrol town and city centres on Friday and Saturday nights, in pairs and teams, often in uniform.
They work with police, councils and nightclubs, but have no police powers.
Volunteers are usually over 18, are members of a local church and receive training in listening, first aid awareness, drugs and alcohol awareness and working with the police.
The aim is often summed up as 'caring, listening and helping'. They do not preach at people, though they will talk about faith if asked.
Listen and talk to people, offer help and advice, and pray if people want it.
Give out flip-flops to people with sore feet, water, blankets, and sometimes food.
Help people who are drunk or vulnerable get home safely, and reduce anti-social behaviour and violence.
Related groups include School Pastors and Prayer Pastors.
The Parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25-37) teaches helping anyone in need.
'Love your neighbour' and 'treat others as you wish to be treated' (Luke 6:31).
Faith without action is dead (James 2:17).
They do not judge people ('Do not judge, or you too will be judged', Matthew 7:1), but offer care to all.

topics.code: Christ Pract.10 (listed as Pract.1 on the school list)
topics.title: The place of mission and evangelism
topics.overview: Mission and evangelism mean spreading the Christian message. Jesus told his followers to do this, and it is a duty for the Church.

bullets: **Mission** is the work of spreading Christianity and showing God's love, including charity and social action.
**Evangelism** is sharing the gospel (the good news about Jesus) through preaching, personal witness and inviting people to faith.
A **missionary** travels to share the faith and often does practical work such as setting up schools, hospitals and wells.
The **Great Commission** (Matthew 28:19-20): Jesus told his followers to 'go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them'.
In Acts 1:8 Jesus told the disciples they would receive the Holy Spirit and be his witnesses to the ends of the earth. At Pentecost the Spirit gave them courage.
Christians believe that Jesus is the way to salvation (John 14:6), so sharing the gospel helps others find eternal life.
Many Christians see all believers as called to witness by words and by example.

**The Alpha Course:** introduces Christianity through a meal, a talk and open discussion where nothing is off limits. It began at Holy Trinity Brompton, London, in 1977 and was developed by Nicky Gumbel from 1990; it is now run worldwide in churches, prisons, workplaces and online.
Missionary organisations, street evangelism, outreach events, social media and TV or radio programmes.
Church-run schools and charities show Christian love in action, which also presents the faith.

views.label: Evangelical/Pentecostal

views.label: Catholic/Anglican
views.text: Mission includes social action, education and care for the poor alongside preaching.

views.label: Some Christians

topics.title: Church growth
topics.overview: The Church is growing in some parts of the world and shrinking in others. Christians use many ways to spread their faith and help the Church grow.

bullets: Christianity is the world's largest religion. It is growing fast in parts of Africa, Asia and South America, especially Pentecostal and charismatic churches.
In Europe and North America many traditional churches are declining, although some new churches and migrant churches are growing.
The school sources say about 80,000 people become Christians each day worldwide. Treat this as a campaign estimate, not a precise fact.
In the 2021 census, 46.2% of people in England and Wales described themselves as Christian, the first time it fell below half (down from 59.3% in 2011), while 37.2% said 'no religion'.

Claims about growth need care: a 2025 Bible Society report ('The Quiet Revival') claimed a big rise in young churchgoers, but in March 2026 the Bible Society said the survey sample behind it was faulty. Other surveys show attendance below pre-pandemic levels (as of 2026).
Lively, welcoming worship, strong community and practical help.
Church planting (starting new churches) and Fresh Expressions such as Messy Church and café churches that reach people who do not attend traditional services.
Use of media: social media, TV, radio and online services.
The Holy Spirit is believed to be at work, and growth follows the Great Commission.

notes.h: Ways individual Christians help the Church grow
bullets: Invite friends to church events and courses such as Alpha.
Pray for others and share personal testimony (their story of faith).
Disciple new converts: train them to follow Jesus and share the faith.
Show Christian love through service so others see their faith.

notes.h: Why Church growth matters to Christians
bullets: It obeys the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19-20).
Christians believe salvation comes through Jesus (John 14:6), so growth means more people can be saved.
A growing Church can do more good: more volunteers and money for food banks, charities and mission.
Growth is also about depth: helping existing members grow in faith (discipleship), not only increasing numbers.
Secularism, busy lives, and a view that church is outdated.
Competing beliefs and criticism of the Church.

views.label: Traditional churches

topics.title: The importance of the worldwide Church and reconciliation
topics.overview: The worldwide Church is made up of Christians everywhere, who work together for peace, unity and reconciliation. The spec asks about working for reconciliation.

bullets: Christians believe they belong to one body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:27), a global community.
Churches help each other through prayer, giving and mission, and work together in groups like the World Council of Churches (ecumenism).
It shows Christian unity and allows the Church to act on big issues like poverty and persecution.
**Reconciliation** means restoring relationships after conflict.
Christians believe God reconciled humans to himself through Jesus (2 Corinthians 5:18-19), so they should reconcile with each other (Matthew 5:23-24).
Jesus taught 'love your enemies' (Matthew 5:44) and 'blessed are the peacemakers' (Matthew 5:9).

Reconciliation can be **personal** (forgiving someone, the Catholic sacrament of reconciliation), between **communities** (Catholics and Protestants in Northern Ireland) or between **nations** (Britain and Germany after the war).

notes.h: Coventry Cathedral and the Community of the Cross of Nails
bullets: Coventry Cathedral was destroyed by German bombing on 14 November 1940. Instead of seeking revenge, Provost Richard Howard had the words **'Father Forgive'** written on the wall of the ruins.

A cross made from medieval roof nails became a symbol of reconciliation. The **Community of the Cross of Nails** now links around 300 churches, schools, charities and peace centres in about 45 countries, including Germany (Coventry Cathedral figures, 2026).
The Coventry **Litany of Reconciliation**, based on the words 'Father forgive', is prayed regularly in Coventry and by partners around the world.
**Corrymeela Community (Northern Ireland):** founded in 1965, a centre where Catholics, Protestants and people of all backgrounds meet to build trust and peace.
**Desmond Tutu:** Anglican Archbishop of Cape Town who opposed apartheid without violence and chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, where victims and offenders could speak and forgive.
**Taize Community (France):** a monastic community that welcomes young Christians of all denominations for prayer and reconciliation.
**Irish Church Peace Project / Pax Christi:** work for peace between groups.

views.label: Catholic
views.text: Reconciliation is also a sacrament: confession restores the relationship with God and the Church. Groups like Pax Christi work for peace.

views.label: Protestant
views.text: Stress the example of Jesus and the Bible, and work through groups like Corrymeela.

topics.title: Christian persecution
topics.overview: Persecution is ill-treatment because of religion. Many Christians around the world face it, and the Church responds with support, prayer and forgiveness.

bullets: **Persecution** is hostility, discrimination or violence because of someone's beliefs.
Forms: attacks on churches and homes, imprisonment, job discrimination, being banned from building churches or sharing faith, and being forced to pay extra taxes. Some are killed for their faith.

Open Doors' 2026 World Watch List estimated that more than 388 million Christians face high levels of persecution and discrimination, about one in seven Christians worldwide. North Korea was ranked the most dangerous country, with others including Somalia, Sudan, Eritrea, Syria, Nigeria and Libya in the top ten.
The school sources claim that most religious persecution today targets Christians; treat this as a claim from campaign groups rather than a fixed fact.
Jesus warned his followers they would be persecuted: 'Blessed are those who are persecuted because of righteousness' (Matthew 5:10).
Persecution can strengthen faith and let Christians share in Jesus' suffering. The early Church grew despite persecution, e.g. the martyrdom of Stephen (Acts 7).
Christians are told to respond with love and forgiveness: 'Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you' (Matthew 5:44) and 'overcome evil with good' (Romans 12:21).
Jesus warned 'If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you' (John 15:20), and Paul wrote that all who want to live a godly life will suffer persecution (2 Timothy 3:12).
Hebrews 13:3 tells Christians to remember prisoners and those ill-treated 'as bound with them', which is why churches pray for and write to persecuted Christians.
Praying for persecuted Christians and speaking out about them.

**Open Doors** supports persecuted Christians with Bibles, training and aid. **Barnabas Fund** sends money. **Christian Solidarity Worldwide (CSW)** campaigns for religious freedom for everyone. **Release International** supports Christians in prison.
Christians campaign to governments and give money, and some smuggle Bibles into closed countries.
Many Christian groups also work for freedom of religion for all, not only Christians.

views.label: Campaigning response
views.text: Supports persecuted believers with practical aid and by lobbying governments for freedom of religion for everyone.

views.label: Forgiving response
views.text: Stresses praying for persecutors, pardoning them and refusing violence, following Jesus on the cross.

topics.title: The Church's response to world poverty
topics.overview: Christians believe they must help the poor. The AQA spec asks about the work of one of CAFOD, Christian Aid or Tearfund.

bullets: Debt, unfair trade, conflict, natural disasters, disease, lack of education and healthcare, and corrupt government.
The spec focuses on the Church's response, but examiners credit knowing why poverty happens.

notes.h: Christian teaching on helping the poor
bullets: Jesus told a rich man to sell his possessions and give to the poor (Mark 10:21).
In the sheep and goats parable, helping the hungry and thirsty is serving Jesus (Matthew 25:35-40).
The parable of the rich man and Lazarus warns against ignoring the poor (Luke 16:19-31). The Good Samaritan teaches love for any person in need.
'Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD' (Proverbs 19:17), and 'faith without action is dead' (James 2:17).

**CAFOD** (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development): founded in 1962 by the Catholic bishops of England and Wales. Provides emergency aid, clean water, healthcare and education, trains communities, and campaigns on issues like climate change and unfair trade. Based on Catholic Social Teaching (human dignity, the common good). Fundraises through Family Fast Day and schools and parishes.

**Christian Aid:** started in 1945 by British and Irish churches to help refugees after the war. Supports long-term development projects and emergency relief, campaigns for justice (tax, climate change) and holds Christian Aid Week each May (red envelopes).

**Tearfund:** an Evangelical charity (founded 1968). Works through local churches to help communities help themselves (e.g. wells, farming, income) and provides disaster relief, supported by prayer and giving. Motto: help people lift themselves out of poverty.
All three give short-term emergency aid and long-term development, and campaign to change unfair systems.

**Short-term aid** is emergency help after a disaster (food, shelter, medicine). **Long-term aid** (development) helps communities support themselves (wells, farming skills, education, small businesses).
**Campaigning** tries to change the causes of poverty, for example unfair trade rules, debt and climate change.

views.text: Stress human dignity, the common good and the preferential option for the poor.

views.text: Work through local churches, combine practical help with sharing the gospel, and stress self-help.

flashcards.q: What is liturgical worship?
flashcards.a: Worship with a set structure and set words, e.g. Catholic Mass, Orthodox Divine Liturgy, Church of England services.

flashcards.q: What is non-liturgical worship?
flashcards.a: Worship with some structure (hymns, readings, sermon) but no fixed words, e.g. many Baptist and Methodist services.

flashcards.q: What is charismatic worship?
flashcards.a: Informal, spontaneous worship led by the Holy Spirit, with clapping, modern music, speaking in tongues. Pentecostal churches.

flashcards.q: How do Quakers worship?
flashcards.a: In silent 'waiting' worship with no leader or set order until someone feels moved by the Spirit to speak.

flashcards.q: Give two features of private worship.
flashcards.a: Prayer and Bible reading alone, using aids like a rosary or icons. Allows a personal relationship with God.

flashcards.q: Which verse supports private prayer?
flashcards.a: Matthew 6:6: go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father.

flashcards.q: Why is the Bible used in worship?
flashcards.a: It teaches about God and his will. Used in readings, sermons and hymns (2 Timothy 3:16).

flashcards.q: What is the Lord's Prayer?
flashcards.a: The prayer Jesus taught his disciples (Matthew 6:9-13), used in worship worldwide.

flashcards.q: What is a set prayer?
flashcards.a: A prayer written down and used repeatedly by many people, e.g. the Lord's Prayer or Hail Mary.

flashcards.q: What is an informal prayer?
flashcards.a: A spontaneous prayer in the person's own words.

flashcards.q: Give four reasons Christians pray.
flashcards.a: To say sorry, thank you, please (ask for help) and to praise God.

flashcards.q: What does 'give us today our daily bread' teach?
flashcards.a: Christians depend on God for daily needs and should pray for help.

flashcards.q: How does the Lord's Prayer link prayer and forgiveness?
flashcards.a: It asks God to forgive us as we forgive others, so Christians must forgive.

flashcards.q: What did St Augustine say a sacrament is?
flashcards.a: An outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace.

flashcards.q: How many sacraments do Catholics recognise?
flashcards.a: Seven: baptism, confirmation, Eucharist, reconciliation, anointing of the sick, marriage, ordination.

flashcards.q: Which two sacraments do most Protestants recognise?
flashcards.a: Baptism and Holy Communion.

flashcards.q: Which Christians have no sacraments?
flashcards.a: Quakers and the Salvation Army.

flashcards.q: What is infant baptism?
flashcards.a: Baptising babies, with water poured or sprinkled in the name of the Trinity. Parents and godparents promise to raise the child in the faith.

flashcards.q: What is believers' baptism?
flashcards.a: Baptising people old enough to choose faith, by full immersion in water. Practised by Baptists and Pentecostals.

flashcards.q: Why do Catholics baptise babies?
flashcards.a: It removes original sin and welcomes the child into the Church.

flashcards.q: What is transubstantiation?
flashcards.a: The Catholic belief that bread and wine become the body and blood of Jesus while keeping their appearance.

flashcards.q: Why do many Protestants see Communion as symbolic?
flashcards.a: They believe the bread and wine remind believers of Jesus' sacrifice at the Last Supper, without changing.

flashcards.q: What is the Orthodox service of Holy Communion called?
flashcards.a: The Divine Liturgy. The sacrament itself is often called the Eucharist or the Holy Mysteries.

flashcards.q: What is the iconostasis?
flashcards.a: The screen of icons in an Orthodox church separating the altar area.

flashcards.q: What is an 'open table'?
flashcards.a: A Communion where all baptised Christians may receive, as in the Methodist Church.

flashcards.q: Which verse tells Christians to remember Jesus at Communion?
flashcards.a: Luke 22:19: 'Do this in remembrance of me.'

flashcards.q: Who saw visions of Mary at Lourdes?
flashcards.a: Bernadette Soubirous, a young girl, in 1858.

flashcards.q: What do pilgrims do at Lourdes?
flashcards.a: Bathe in or drink the spring water, pray at the Grotto, join the torchlight procession and Rosary, and help the sick.

flashcards.q: What is special about Iona?
flashcards.a: St Columba founded a monastery there in 563 AD. It is a quiet place for prayer, reflection and the Iona Community's work for peace.

flashcards.q: What is a pilgrimage?
flashcards.a: A journey to a holy place for religious reasons.

flashcards.q: Give one contrast between Lourdes and Iona.
flashcards.a: Lourdes: Catholic, healing and crowds. Iona: ecumenical, quiet and reflective.

flashcards.q: Give two reasons for going on pilgrimage.
flashcards.a: To grow closer to God and to seek healing or forgiveness.

flashcards.q: What does Christmas celebrate?
flashcards.a: The birth of Jesus, the incarnation: God becoming human.

flashcards.q: What is Advent?
flashcards.a: The weeks before Christmas, a time of waiting and preparation.

flashcards.q: What happens on Maundy Thursday?
flashcards.a: Christians remember the Last Supper and Jesus washing the disciples' feet.

flashcards.q: What is Good Friday?
flashcards.a: The day Jesus was crucified; services are solemn and churches are bare.

flashcards.q: What do Easter eggs and the Paschal candle symbolise?
flashcards.a: New life and the risen Jesus, the light of the world.

flashcards.q: Why is Easter more important than Christmas to many Christians?
flashcards.a: It celebrates the resurrection, the foundation of the Christian faith.

flashcards.q: What is a food bank?
flashcards.a: A charity that gives free emergency food parcels to people who cannot afford food.

flashcards.q: Name a Christian charity that runs food banks.
flashcards.a: The Trussell Trust.

flashcards.q: Which parable supports feeding the hungry?
flashcards.a: The sheep and the goats: 'I was hungry and you gave me something to eat' (Matthew 25:35).

flashcards.q: Give two ways a local church helps its community.
flashcards.a: Runs a food bank and youth or toddler groups, or offers pastoral care, luncheon clubs and a community hall.

flashcards.q: Which verse says faith needs action?
flashcards.a: James 2:17.

flashcards.q: What is the Oasis Project?
flashcards.a: A Plymouth Methodist project offering food support, a job club, training and advice.

flashcards.q: When and where did Street Pastors begin?
flashcards.a: 2003 in Brixton, London.

flashcards.q: Who are Street Pastors?
flashcards.a: Trained Christian volunteers who patrol town centres at night to care for and listen to people.

flashcards.q: Give two things Street Pastors give out.
flashcards.a: Flip-flops, water, blankets or food.

flashcards.q: Which parable motivates Street Pastors?
flashcards.a: The Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25-37).

flashcards.q: Which verse tells Christians not to judge?
flashcards.a: Matthew 7:1.

flashcards.q: Who do Street Pastors work with?
flashcards.a: Police, councils and nightclub staff.

flashcards.q: What is evangelism?
flashcards.a: Spreading the gospel to persuade people to follow Jesus.

flashcards.q: What is the Great Commission?
flashcards.a: Jesus' command to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19-20).

flashcards.q: What is the Alpha Course?
flashcards.a: A course introducing Christianity through a meal, a talk and discussion, run in churches, prisons and workplaces.

flashcards.q: Who gave the disciples courage to spread the gospel?
flashcards.a: The Holy Spirit at Pentecost.

flashcards.q: What is a missionary?
flashcards.a: A person who spreads Christianity, often abroad, and does practical work such as schools and wells.

flashcards.q: Which verse says 'You will be my witnesses'?
flashcards.a: Acts 1:8.

flashcards.q: Where is the Church growing fastest?
flashcards.a: Africa, Asia and South America.

flashcards.q: What is church planting?
flashcards.a: Starting new churches in new places.

flashcards.q: Give two ways Christians spread the faith.
flashcards.a: Social media, inviting people to events or Alpha, sharing their story, and praying for others.

flashcards.q: What is Messy Church?
flashcards.a: A Fresh Expression of church for families, with crafts, activities and a meal.

flashcards.q: What is a convert?
flashcards.a: Someone who has changed to a new religion or belief.

flashcards.q: Why is Church growth important to Christians?
flashcards.a: It follows the Great Commission and spreads God's love and salvation.

flashcards.q: What is reconciliation?
flashcards.a: Restoring harmony after relationships have broken down.

flashcards.q: What is Corrymeela?
flashcards.a: A community in Northern Ireland that brings together Catholics, Protestants and others to build trust and peace.

flashcards.q: Who was Desmond Tutu?
flashcards.a: Anglican Archbishop of Cape Town who opposed apartheid non-violently and chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

flashcards.q: Which verse says God was reconciling the world to himself?
flashcards.a: 2 Corinthians 5:19.

flashcards.q: What is ecumenism?
flashcards.a: Working for unity between Christian denominations.

flashcards.q: Which Beatitude praises peacemakers?
flashcards.a: Matthew 5:9: 'Blessed are the peacemakers.'

flashcards.q: What is persecution?
flashcards.a: Hostility or ill-treatment because of religion.

flashcards.q: Give two examples of Christian persecution.
flashcards.a: Attacks on churches, imprisonment, job discrimination, bans on building churches or murder.

flashcards.q: Which verse says the persecuted are blessed?
flashcards.a: Matthew 5:10.

flashcards.q: Name two charities that help persecuted Christians.
flashcards.a: Open Doors and the Barnabas Fund (also CSW and Release International).

flashcards.q: How does Jesus say to treat persecutors?
flashcards.a: Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matthew 5:44).

flashcards.q: Name a country where Christians are persecuted.
flashcards.a: North Korea, Somalia, Nigeria or Libya.

flashcards.q: What does CAFOD stand for?
flashcards.a: Catholic Agency for Overseas Development.

flashcards.q: When was Christian Aid started?
flashcards.a: 1945, by British and Irish churches to help refugees after the war.

flashcards.q: What type of church is Tearfund linked to?
flashcards.a: Evangelical churches.

flashcards.q: Give two causes of poverty.
flashcards.a: Debt, conflict, unfair trade, natural disasters, disease or lack of education.

flashcards.q: Which verse says to sell what you have and give to the poor?
flashcards.a: Mark 10:21.

flashcards.q: Give two things Christian charities do.
flashcards.a: Emergency relief, long-term development projects, clean water, campaigning against unfair trade.

flashcards.q: Which verse describes what the first Christians did when they met?
flashcards.a: Acts 2:42: the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer.

flashcards.q: What is a lectionary?
flashcards.a: A set cycle of Bible readings for each service, used in Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches.

flashcards.q: Give one strength and one weakness of liturgical worship.
flashcards.a: Strength: the same words unite Christians worldwide and across history. Weakness: it can become routine if said without thinking.

flashcards.q: What does ACTS stand for in prayer?
flashcards.a: Adoration, Confession, Thanksgiving, Supplication (asking).

flashcards.q: What is intercession?
flashcards.a: Praying for other people, for example the sick, the bereaved or people in war zones.

flashcards.q: Why do some Christians prefer informal prayer to set prayer?
flashcards.a: It is personal and sincere, and Jesus warned against 'vain repetitions' (Matthew 6:7).

flashcards.q: What do the candle and white garment symbolise at infant baptism?
flashcards.a: Candle: passing from darkness to the light of Christ. White garment: new life and being washed clean of sin.

flashcards.q: What is a baptistery?
flashcards.a: A pool in some churches (for example Baptist) used for full-immersion believers' baptism.

flashcards.q: What is confirmation?
flashcards.a: A service (sacrament for Catholics) where a young person or adult confirms for themselves the promises made at their baptism.

flashcards.q: What does 'Eucharist' mean?
flashcards.a: Thanksgiving (from Greek). Christians give thanks for Jesus' sacrifice.

flashcards.q: What do Lutherans believe about Communion?
flashcards.a: Christ is truly present 'in, with and under' the bread and wine, which remain bread and wine (sometimes called consubstantiation).

flashcards.q: Which verse shows Communion unites believers as one body?
flashcards.a: 1 Corinthians 10:17: 'there is one loaf of bread, we, who are many, are one body'.

flashcards.q: How many healings at Lourdes has the Catholic Church officially recognised as miracles?
flashcards.a: 72 (the 72nd was announced in 2025), after medical checks by the Lourdes Medical Bureau.

flashcards.q: Who founded the Iona Community and when?
flashcards.a: George MacLeod, a Church of Scotland minister, in 1938.

flashcards.q: Is pilgrimage compulsory for Christians?
flashcards.a: No. It is a personal choice to deepen faith, unlike Hajj, which is a duty in Islam.

flashcards.q: What is a Christingle?
flashcards.a: An orange (the world) with a candle (Jesus, light of the world), a red ribbon (his blood) and fruit or sweets on sticks (God's gifts and the four seasons), used in Advent and Christmas services.

flashcards.q: What is Ash Wednesday?
flashcards.a: The first day of Lent. Many Christians receive a cross of ash on the forehead as a sign of sorrow for sin.

flashcards.q: How is the date of Easter set?
flashcards.a: The first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the spring equinox (between 22 March and 25 April in Western churches).

flashcards.q: Roughly how many emergency food parcels did Trussell food banks give out in 2025?
flashcards.a: About 2.6 million, around 900,000 of them for children (Trussell figures published 2026).

flashcards.q: How do people usually get help from a Trussell food bank?
flashcards.a: They are referred by a professional such as a doctor, social worker or school, and receive a voucher for a parcel.

flashcards.q: Give three ways churches serve their local community apart from food banks.
flashcards.a: Youth and toddler groups, lunch clubs or coffee mornings for lonely people, debt advice, night shelters, warm spaces, a quiet place to pray.

flashcards.q: Which organisation started Street Pastors?
flashcards.a: The Ascension Trust, led by Rev Les Isaac, in 2003.

flashcards.q: What three words sum up what Street Pastors do?
flashcards.a: Caring, listening and helping.

flashcards.q: Do Street Pastors try to convert people on the street?
flashcards.a: No. They offer care and safety; they will talk or pray about faith only if people ask.

flashcards.q: Where and when did the Alpha Course begin?
flashcards.a: At Holy Trinity Brompton, London, in 1977; developed by Nicky Gumbel from 1990.

flashcards.q: Which verse tells Christians to be ready to explain their hope?
flashcards.a: 1 Peter 3:15.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between mission and evangelism?
flashcards.a: Mission is the wider task of serving and sharing God's love (including social action). Evangelism is spreading the gospel to bring people to faith.

flashcards.q: What did the 2021 census show about Christianity in England and Wales?
flashcards.a: 46.2% described themselves as Christian, the first time below half (59.3% in 2011); 37.2% said 'no religion'.

flashcards.q: Why should you be careful about claims of a 'quiet revival' in British churches?
flashcards.a: The 2025 Bible Society report was based on a survey sample the Bible Society said in March 2026 was faulty; other surveys show attendance below pre-pandemic levels.

flashcards.q: Which parable of Jesus is about something small growing large?
flashcards.a: The mustard seed (Matthew 13:31-32).

flashcards.q: What happened at Coventry Cathedral in 1940 and how did it respond?
flashcards.a: It was destroyed by bombing on 14 November 1940. Provost Richard Howard had 'Father Forgive' written in the ruins and worked for reconciliation with Germany.

flashcards.q: What is the Community of the Cross of Nails?
flashcards.a: A worldwide network, led from Coventry Cathedral, of around 300 churches, schools and peace centres working for reconciliation.

flashcards.q: Which verse says to be reconciled to your brother before offering your gift at the altar?
flashcards.a: Matthew 5:23-24.

flashcards.q: About how many Christians did Open Doors' 2026 World Watch List say face high levels of persecution?
flashcards.a: More than 388 million, about one in seven Christians worldwide. North Korea was ranked first.

flashcards.q: Who was the first Christian martyr and how did he respond?
flashcards.a: Stephen (Acts 7). As he was stoned he prayed 'Lord, don't hold this sin against them!'

flashcards.q: Which verse tells Christians to remember prisoners as if they were in prison with them?
flashcards.a: Hebrews 13:3.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between short-term and long-term aid?
flashcards.a: Short-term (emergency) aid meets immediate needs after a disaster. Long-term (development) aid helps communities support themselves, for example wells, farming skills and education.

flashcards.q: When is Christian Aid Week?
flashcards.a: Every May, when volunteers collect money house to house using red envelopes.

flashcards.q: When was Tearfund founded and how does it work?
flashcards.a: 1968, by the Evangelical Alliance. It works through local churches to help communities lift themselves out of poverty.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is a feature of liturgical worship?
options: A set order and set words
quiz.why: Liturgical worship follows a fixed structure.

quiz.q: Which Christians practise silent 'waiting' worship?
quiz.why: Quakers wait in silence until moved by the Spirit.

quiz.q: A Christian reads the Bible and prays alone in her bedroom. This is:
quiz.why: Private worship is done alone or at home.

quiz.q: Who taught the Lord's Prayer?
quiz.why: Jesus taught it to his disciples (Matthew 6:9-13).

quiz.q: A prayer written down and used by many people is called:
quiz.why: Set prayers include the Lord's Prayer.

quiz.q: Which part of the Lord's Prayer asks for forgiveness?
options: Forgive us our sins as we forgive those who sin against us
Give us today our daily bread
quiz.why: It links being forgiven to forgiving others.

quiz.q: Which of these denominations practises believers' baptism?
quiz.why: Baptists baptise believers by full immersion.

quiz.q: How many sacraments do Roman Catholics recognise?
quiz.why: Seven sacraments.

quiz.q: Which verse commands baptism in the name of the Trinity?
quiz.why: Matthew 28:19, the Great Commission.

quiz.q: Transubstantiation is a belief held by:
quiz.why: Catholics believe bread and wine become Jesus' body and blood.

quiz.q: In a Methodist service the wine is:
options: Alcoholic and drunk by the priest only
quiz.why: Methodists use non-alcoholic wine and an open table.

quiz.q: What did Jesus say at the Last Supper about the bread?
quiz.why: Matthew 26:26: 'Take and eat; this is my body.'

quiz.q: Who is linked with the visions at Lourdes?
quiz.why: Bernadette saw Mary in 1858.

quiz.q: Iona is most closely linked to which saint?
quiz.why: St Columba founded a monastery there in 563.

quiz.q: Which statement best contrasts Lourdes and Iona?
options: Lourdes is about healing; Iona is quiet and reflective
quiz.why: Lourdes: healing and crowds. Iona: peace and reflection.

quiz.q: Which day of Holy Week commemorates the crucifixion?
quiz.why: Good Friday.

quiz.q: Christmas celebrates:
quiz.why: God becoming human in Jesus.

quiz.q: Why are palm crosses given on Palm Sunday?
options: To remember Jesus' entry into Jerusalem
quiz.why: They recall crowds waving palms.

quiz.q: Which charity runs a large network of UK food banks?
quiz.why: The Trussell Trust.

quiz.q: Which parable is most linked to feeding the hungry?
quiz.why: Matthew 25:35-40.

quiz.q: Why do many churches run food banks?
options: To follow Jesus' teaching to help the needy
quiz.why: Christians run food banks because Jesus taught that feeding the hungry is serving him (Matthew 25:35-40). Food banks help anyone, with no requirement to attend church.

quiz.q: Street Pastors patrol on:
quiz.why: They work on weekend nights when town centres are busy.

quiz.q: Which item do Street Pastors hand out?
quiz.why: They give flip-flops, water and blankets.

quiz.q: Street Pastors were first set up in:
quiz.why: Founded in Brixton in 2003.

quiz.q: The Great Commission is found in:
quiz.why: Matthew 28:19-20.

quiz.q: Which is a feature of the Alpha Course?
options: A meal, a talk and open discussion
quiz.why: Alpha invites questions about Christianity.

quiz.q: Evangelism means:
quiz.why: Sharing the good news about Jesus.

quiz.q: In which region is the Church currently growing fastest?
quiz.why: Africa, Asia and South America.

quiz.q: Messy Church is an example of:
quiz.why: It reaches families who do not attend traditional services.

quiz.q: Which verse links to church growth after Pentecost?
quiz.why: About three thousand were added.

quiz.q: Reconciliation means:
quiz.why: Bringing people back together.

quiz.q: Corrymeela is in:
quiz.why: A peace centre for Catholics and Protestants.

quiz.q: Desmond Tutu opposed:
quiz.why: He campaigned against apartheid in South Africa.

quiz.q: Which charity supports persecuted Christians?
quiz.why: Open Doors, also the Barnabas Fund.

quiz.q: How does Jesus tell Christians to treat persecutors?
options: Love them and pray for them
quiz.why: Matthew 5:44.

quiz.q: Persecution means:
quiz.why: It is hostility due to belief.

quiz.q: CAFOD is supported mainly by which Christians?
quiz.why: Catholic Agency for Overseas Development.

quiz.q: Which charity was set up by UK and Irish churches in 1945?
quiz.why: Christian Aid began to help refugees after WWII.

quiz.q: Which teaching is used to support helping the poor?
quiz.why: Jesus told a rich man to give to the poor.

quiz.q: Which type of worship would you most expect in a Pentecostal church?
quiz.why: Pentecostal worship is informal and lively, with modern songs and gifts of the Spirit.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is an example of private worship?
options: Praying the rosary alone at home
quiz.why: Private worship is done alone. Choirs, groups and Mass are public worship.

quiz.q: Which source supports Christians meeting together for worship?
quiz.why: Hebrews 10:25 tells Christians not to give up meeting together.

quiz.q: Which line of the Lord's Prayer asks God to provide for daily needs?
options: Give us today our daily bread
quiz.why: 'Daily bread' stands for everything people need each day.

quiz.q: A Christian prays for victims of a flood. This type of prayer is called:
quiz.why: Intercession is praying on behalf of other people.

quiz.q: Which source shows Jesus praying privately?
quiz.why: Mark 1:35: Jesus went to a deserted place early in the morning to pray.

quiz.q: Which source is most used to support believers' baptism?
quiz.why: Acts 2:38 links baptism to repentance, which a baby cannot do.

quiz.q: In infant baptism, who make promises on the baby's behalf?
quiz.why: Parents and godparents promise to bring the child up as a Christian.

quiz.q: Which of these is a purpose of baptism, rather than a feature?
quiz.why: Purposes are reasons (cleansing from sin, joining the Church); the others are features of the ceremony.

quiz.q: In which church is Communion given to the people on a spoon, with bread and wine together?
quiz.why: Orthodox Christians receive bread soaked in wine from a spoon, and even infants receive.

quiz.q: Which Christians do NOT celebrate Communion as a sacrament?
quiz.why: The Salvation Army and Quakers do not use outward sacraments.

quiz.q: What does 'Eucharist' mean?
quiz.why: Eucharist comes from the Greek for thanksgiving.

quiz.q: Which pilgrimage site is in Scotland?
quiz.why: Iona is an island off the west coast of Scotland.

quiz.q: Walsingham in Norfolk is a pilgrimage site linked to:
quiz.why: Walsingham is a shrine to Mary used by Catholics and Anglicans.

quiz.q: Which source shows that Jesus' family went on pilgrimage?
quiz.why: Luke 2:41: his parents went to Jerusalem every year for Passover.

quiz.q: What does the Paschal candle lit at the Easter Vigil represent?
options: The risen Christ, light of the world
quiz.why: The Paschal candle represents Jesus risen from the dead, the light that overcomes darkness.

quiz.q: Which day begins Lent?
quiz.why: Lent begins on Ash Wednesday and lasts forty days (not counting Sundays).

quiz.q: A student says Christians celebrate Easter 'because of chocolate eggs'. What is the best correction?
options: Christians celebrate the resurrection of Jesus
Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus
Christians celebrate the coming of spring only
quiz.why: Easter celebrates the resurrection; eggs are a symbol of new life, not the reason.

quiz.q: Which Bible teaching is most directly linked to running food banks?
options: 'I was hungry, and you gave me food'
'Be still, and know that I am God'
quiz.why: Matthew 25:35, from the sheep and the goats.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is an example of the Church in the LOCAL community?
quiz.why: A youth club serves the local area; the others are worldwide work.

quiz.q: Which statement about Street Pastors is correct?
options: They work with the police but have no police powers
They arrest people who are drunk
They only work on Sunday mornings
quiz.why: They are trained church volunteers who cooperate with police and councils.

quiz.q: Which parable best explains why Street Pastors help strangers?
quiz.why: The Good Samaritan helped a stranger in need, and Jesus said 'Go and do likewise'.

quiz.q: Which source tells Christians they will be Jesus' witnesses 'to the uttermost parts of the earth'?
quiz.why: Acts 1:8, spoken just before the ascension.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is evangelism?
options: Explaining the gospel at an Alpha Course
quiz.why: Evangelism is sharing the good news of Jesus to bring people to faith.

quiz.q: According to the 2021 census, roughly what percentage of people in England and Wales described themselves as Christian?
A church starts a new congregation in a café on a housing estate. This is called:
quiz.why: Church planting means starting new churches in new places.

quiz.q: Which reason for Church growth is based on Jesus' command?
quiz.why: Matthew 28:19-20: 'make disciples of all nations'.

quiz.q: Which words were written on the ruined wall of Coventry Cathedral?
quiz.why: Provost Richard Howard chose 'Father Forgive' rather than calling for revenge.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of personal reconciliation?
options: Two friends forgiving each other after an argument
The Community of the Cross of Nails
quiz.why: Personal reconciliation is between individuals; the others are organised or national.

quiz.q: Which charity publishes the yearly World Watch List?
quiz.why: Open Doors ranks the countries where Christians face most persecution.

quiz.q: Which source best supports Christians forgiving their persecutors?
quiz.why: 'Love your enemies... pray for those who persecute you'.

quiz.q: Which charity holds a 'Family Fast Day' and is supported by the Catholic Church?
quiz.why: CAFOD's Family Fast Days are held in Lent and autumn.

quiz.q: Digging a well so a village has clean water for years is an example of:
quiz.why: Long-term (development) aid helps communities support themselves.

truefalse.s: Quaker meetings for worship usually have no set leader or order.
truefalse.why: Quakers wait in silence until someone feels moved to speak.

truefalse.s: Going to a Bible study group is an example of private worship.
truefalse.why: A group is public or communal worship. Private worship is done alone.

truefalse.s: Liturgical worship follows a set pattern of words and actions.
truefalse.why: For example the Catholic Mass or Anglican Common Worship.

truefalse.s: The Bible is only used in Protestant worship.
truefalse.why: All main traditions read the Bible in worship; Catholics and Anglicans use a lectionary.

truefalse.s: The Lord's Prayer was taught by Jesus.
truefalse.why: Matthew 6:9-13 and Luke 11:2-4.

truefalse.s: Informal prayer must use words written by the Church.
truefalse.why: Informal prayer uses the person's own words; set prayers use written words.

truefalse.s: Supplication means asking God for help.
truefalse.why: It is the S in ACTS.

truefalse.s: Christians believe they can only pray inside a church.
truefalse.why: Christians can pray anywhere, any time (1 Thessalonians 5:17: pray without ceasing).

truefalse.s: Baptists baptise babies by sprinkling water on their heads.
truefalse.why: Baptists practise believers' baptism by full immersion.

truefalse.s: Catholics believe baptism removes original sin.
truefalse.why: This is one main reason Catholics baptise infants.

truefalse.s: Orthodox Christians immerse babies at baptism.
truefalse.why: Orthodox infant baptism is usually by triple immersion.

truefalse.s: Quakers and the Salvation Army baptise with water.
truefalse.why: They do not use outward sacraments; they stress inner, spiritual baptism.

truefalse.s: A sacrament is an outward sign of an inward grace.
truefalse.why: This is St Augustine's definition.

truefalse.s: All Christians believe the bread and wine become Jesus' body and blood.
truefalse.why: Transubstantiation is Catholic. Many Protestants see Communion as a symbolic memorial.

truefalse.s: Communion remembers the Last Supper.
truefalse.why: Jesus said 'Do this in memory of me' (Luke 22:19).

truefalse.s: Methodists often use non-alcoholic wine in small individual cups.
truefalse.why: Methodists have a tradition of not drinking alcohol.

truefalse.s: The Orthodox Church only gives Communion to adults.
truefalse.why: Orthodox Christians give Communion to baptised infants and children too.

truefalse.s: Bernadette said she saw the Virgin Mary at Lourdes in 1858.
truefalse.why: She reported 18 appearances in the Grotto.

truefalse.s: Iona is a Catholic-only pilgrimage site.
truefalse.why: The Iona Community is ecumenical, welcoming all denominations.

truefalse.s: Every pilgrim who visits Lourdes is physically healed.
truefalse.why: Only a small number of cures are recognised; many pilgrims speak of spiritual healing and peace instead.

truefalse.s: St Columba founded a monastery on Iona in AD 563.
truefalse.why: From there Christianity spread across Scotland and northern England.

truefalse.s: Christmas celebrates the incarnation.
truefalse.why: It remembers God becoming human in the birth of Jesus.

truefalse.s: Good Friday services are usually joyful, with flowers and bells.
truefalse.why: Good Friday is solemn: churches are often bare. Joyful services are on Easter Day.

truefalse.s: Easter is on the same date every year.
truefalse.why: Easter moves: it depends on the full moon after the spring equinox.

truefalse.s: Many Christians see Easter as more important than Christmas.
truefalse.why: The resurrection is the foundation of Christian faith (1 Corinthians 15:14).

truefalse.s: Lent is part of how Christians celebrate Easter Day itself.
truefalse.why: Lent is the time of preparation before Easter. The examiners noted students confusing the two in 2023.

truefalse.s: Most Trussell food banks are run by paid government staff.
truefalse.why: They are run mainly by volunteers, many from local churches.

truefalse.s: Churches may open their buildings as warm spaces in winter.
truefalse.why: This is one way churches serve their community.

truefalse.s: Food banks are an example of the Church's work in the worldwide community.
truefalse.why: Food banks are local, UK-based work; overseas work is done by charities such as CAFOD.

truefalse.s: Some Christians argue churches should also campaign so that food banks are not needed.
truefalse.why: They see tackling the causes of poverty as part of justice.

truefalse.s: Street Pastors began in Brixton, London, in 2003.
truefalse.why: Started by the Ascension Trust and Rev Les Isaac.

truefalse.s: Street Pastors hand out flip-flops to people struggling to walk in high heels.
truefalse.why: A well-known example of practical care.

truefalse.s: Street Pastors have the power to arrest people.
truefalse.why: They have no police powers; they work alongside police.

truefalse.s: Street Pastors only help people who go to church.
truefalse.why: They help anyone in need, without judging (Matthew 7:1).

truefalse.s: The Great Commission is in Matthew 28.
truefalse.why: Matthew 28:19-20.

truefalse.s: Evangelism and mission mean exactly the same thing.
truefalse.why: Mission is wider (service and sharing God's love); evangelism is sharing the gospel.

truefalse.s: The Alpha Course includes a meal and open discussion.
truefalse.why: Guests eat together, hear a talk and discuss freely.

truefalse.s: Some Christians prefer to witness by example rather than by trying to convert people.
truefalse.why: They stress respect for others' beliefs and showing faith through actions.

truefalse.s: The Church is growing fastest in Western Europe.
truefalse.why: Growth is fastest in Africa, Asia and South America; many European churches are declining.

truefalse.s: Messy Church is a Fresh Expression aimed at families.
truefalse.why: It uses crafts, activities and a meal to reach families.

truefalse.s: Church growth only means more people attending services.
truefalse.why: It can also mean growing in faith (discipleship) and in service to the community.

truefalse.s: Acts 2:41 says about three thousand were added to the Church after Peter's Pentecost sermon.
truefalse.why: This shows growth in the early Church.

truefalse.s: Reconciliation means restoring relationships after conflict.
truefalse.why: This is the key definition.

truefalse.s: Corrymeela is in South Africa.
truefalse.why: Corrymeela is in Northern Ireland. Desmond Tutu worked in South Africa.

truefalse.s: Catholics have a sacrament called reconciliation.
truefalse.why: Confession restores the relationship with God and the Church.

truefalse.s: Desmond Tutu used violence to end apartheid.
truefalse.why: He opposed apartheid non-violently and later chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

truefalse.s: Persecution means ill-treatment because of someone's beliefs.
truefalse.why: It can include violence, imprisonment and discrimination.

truefalse.s: Jesus promised his followers they would never be persecuted.
truefalse.why: He warned 'If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you' (John 15:20).

truefalse.s: Christian Solidarity Worldwide campaigns for religious freedom for people of all faiths.
truefalse.why: CSW works for freedom of religion or belief for everyone.

truefalse.s: The Church grew in its early years despite persecution.
truefalse.why: After Stephen's death believers scattered and spread the faith (Acts 8).

truefalse.s: CAFOD is the official aid agency of the Catholic Church in England and Wales.
truefalse.why: It was founded by the bishops in 1962.

truefalse.s: Christian Aid only gives help to Christians.
truefalse.why: It helps people of all faiths and none, based on need.

truefalse.s: Christian charities only give emergency aid.
truefalse.why: They also give long-term development aid and campaign against causes of poverty.

truefalse.s: Tearfund works through local churches in the countries it helps.
truefalse.why: It partners with local churches to mobilise communities.

short.q: Give one example of private worship.
short.a: Praying alone at home (accept: reading the Bible alone, using a rosary alone, meditating on an icon, singing worship songs alone)

short.q: Name one denomination that uses liturgical worship.
short.a: Catholic (accept: Orthodox, Church of England / Anglican)

short.q: Give one feature of non-liturgical worship.
short.a: A sermon at the centre (accept: hymns chosen by the minister, free prayers, Bible readings chosen for the day, no fixed words)

short.q: Give one example of a set prayer.
short.a: The Lord's Prayer (accept: the Hail Mary, the Grace, the Jesus Prayer, collects)

short.q: Give one reason Christians pray.
short.a: To praise God (accept: to say sorry, to thank God, to ask for help, to pray for others, to feel close to God)

short.q: Give one phrase from the Lord's Prayer.
