exam.q: Explain two different ways Christians worship. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is liturgical worship, used by Catholics and Anglicans. It follows a set order with set prayers and responses, such as the Mass. This helps worshippers feel united with Christians across the world and focus on God through a familiar pattern. A different way is informal charismatic worship, used by Pentecostals. It has no fixed order and includes spontaneous prayer, clapping and speaking in tongues, because they believe the Holy Spirit leads the service.
points: Liturgical: set order and words, e.g. Catholic Mass
Non-liturgical: hymns, readings and sermon, no fixed words
Informal charismatic: spontaneous, Spirit-led, Pentecostal
Waiting worship: Quaker silence
Private worship: prayer and Bible reading alone

exam.q: Explain two different types of prayer used by Christians. (4 marks)
exam.model: One type is set prayer, such as the Lord's Prayer, which has been written down and used by many Christians. It is familiar and unites believers, and helps those who find it hard to find words. A different type is informal prayer, which is in the person's own words. It is spontaneous and personal, so Christians can speak honestly to God about their own needs at any time.
points: Set prayers: written, shared, e.g. Lord's Prayer, Hail Mary
Informal prayers: own words, spontaneous, personal
Silent or private prayer
Reasons: unity or personal relationship

exam.q: Explain two different types of baptism. (4 marks)
exam.model: One type is infant baptism, practised by Catholics and Anglicans. Water is poured or sprinkled on a baby in the name of the Trinity, and parents and godparents promise to raise the child as a Christian. Catholics believe it removes original sin. A different type is believers' baptism, practised by Baptists. A person old enough to choose faith is fully immersed in water, because they believe baptism should follow a personal decision to follow Jesus.
points: Infant baptism: babies, water poured, godparents, removes original sin
Believers' baptism: adults or older children, full immersion, personal choice
Reasons from the Bible: Mark 10:14 or Acts 2:38
Denominations: Catholic, Anglican; Baptist, Pentecostal

exam.q: Explain two different Christian beliefs about the meaning of Holy Communion. (4 marks)
exam.model: One belief, held by Catholics, is transubstantiation. This means the bread and wine become the body and blood of Jesus during the Mass, even though they look the same, because Jesus said 'this is my body'. A different belief, held by many Protestants such as Baptists, is that the bread and wine are only symbols. They believe Communion is a memorial of the Last Supper that reminds them of Jesus' sacrifice.
points: Catholic: transubstantiation, real presence
Orthodox: real presence as a mystery
Protestant: symbolic memorial
Quakers and Salvation Army: no Communion

exam.q: Explain two contrasting types of Christian pilgrimage. (4 marks)
exam.model: One type is a pilgrimage to Lourdes in France, where Catholics visit the spring linked to Bernadette's visions of Mary. Pilgrims bathe in the water, pray at the Grotto and join the torchlight procession, often hoping for healing. A contrasting type is a pilgrimage to Iona, a quiet island in Scotland. Pilgrims there stay in the community, attend worship in the abbey and spend time in reflection and prayer, seeking peace rather than healing.
points: Lourdes: Mary, healing spring, Grotto, procession
Iona: St Columba, quiet reflection, Iona Community
Contrast: Catholic vs ecumenical; healing vs peace
Other: Jerusalem, Rome

exam.q: Explain two different ways Christians celebrate Easter. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is by attending special services in Holy Week, such as the solemn Good Friday service. Churches are stripped bare and the Stations of the Cross are followed to remember Jesus' death. A different way is by joyful celebrations on Easter Sunday, such as decorating the church with flowers and singing hymns, because Christians believe Jesus has risen. Some also give Easter eggs to symbolise new life.
points: Good Friday: solemn services, bare church, Stations of the Cross
Easter Sunday: joyful services, flowers, 'Christ is risen'
Easter Vigil and Paschal candle
Easter eggs and family meals
Lent and Palm Sunday observances

exam.q: Explain two ways in which churches help their local communities. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One way is by running food banks. Many churches host collection points and volunteers who give emergency parcels to people who cannot afford food, often through the Trussell Trust. In Matthew 25:35 Jesus says 'I was hungry and you gave me something to eat'. This means that Christians believe helping the hungry is serving Jesus, so churches see food banks as part of their faith. Another way is through Street Pastors, trained volunteers who patrol at night to care for vulnerable people. Luke 10:37 ends the parable of the Good Samaritan with 'Go and do likewise'. This means Christians believe they should help anyone in need.
points: Food banks: parcels, volunteers, Trussell Trust
Street Pastors: patrols, flip-flops, listening
Other: youth groups, toddler groups, pastoral care
Sources: Matthew 25:35-40, Luke 10:37, James 2:17, Mark 12:31
Application: serving others as serving Jesus

exam.q: Explain two reasons why Christians support Street Pastors. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One reason is that Jesus taught Christians to help anyone in need. In the parable of the Good Samaritan a stranger helps an injured man, and Jesus says 'Go and do likewise' (Luke 10:37). This means Christians should help people on the streets, so Street Pastors give out water, flip-flops and offer a listening ear. Another reason is that Christians believe faith must be shown through action. James 2:17 says 'faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead'. This means Christians cannot just pray, so volunteers give up weekend nights to make town centres safer.
points: Good Samaritan: help anyone in need
Faith in action, James 2:17
Love your neighbour, Mark 12:31
Golden Rule, Luke 6:31
Do not judge, Matthew 7:1

exam.q: Explain two reasons why Christians believe mission and evangelism are important. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One reason is that Jesus commanded his followers to spread the gospel. In Matthew 28:19 he says 'go and make disciples of all nations'. This is called the Great Commission, so Christians believe they have a duty to share their faith and help others become Christians, for example through the Alpha Course. Another reason is that Christians believe faith in Jesus leads to salvation. Jesus said 'I am the way and the truth and the life' (John 14:6). This means Christians want others to find eternal life, so some become missionaries and tell people about Jesus.
points: Great Commission: make disciples
Salvation through Jesus
Holy Spirit at Pentecost gave courage
Sources: Matthew 28:19, Mark 16:15, Acts 1:8, John 14:6
Examples: Alpha Course, missionaries

exam.q: Explain two ways Christians work for reconciliation. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One way is through communities like Corrymeela in Northern Ireland. It brings Catholics and Protestants together at its centre to build trust and understand each other. Jesus said 'Blessed are the peacemakers' (Matthew 5:9). This means Christians should actively work for peace, so Corrymeela helps divided groups move away from violence. Another way is through people like Desmond Tutu, who led the Truth and Reconciliation Commission in South Africa, where victims could tell their stories and offenders could ask forgiveness. 2 Corinthians 5:19 says God was reconciling the world to himself in Christ. This means Christians should reconcile with each other.
points: Corrymeela: Catholics and Protestants meet
Desmond Tutu and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission
Irish Church Peace Project or Pax Christi
Sources: Matthew 5:9, Matthew 5:44, 2 Corinthians 5:18-19
Application: forgiveness and peacemaking

exam.q: Explain two ways the Church responds to the persecution of Christians. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One way is by giving practical help. Charities like Open Doors supply Bibles and support to persecuted Christians, and the Barnabas Fund sends money. 1 Corinthians 12:26 says 'if one part suffers, every part suffers with it'. This means Christians feel they must help fellow believers because they are one body. Another way is by responding with forgiveness and prayer. Jesus said 'Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you' (Matthew 5:44). This means Christians do not take revenge, but pray for persecutors and campaign for religious freedom through groups like CSW.
points: Practical help: Open Doors, Barnabas Fund
Campaigning: CSW, Release International
Prayer and forgiveness
Sources: Matthew 5:10, Matthew 5:44, Romans 12:21, 1 Corinthians 12:26

exam.q: Explain two ways in which Christian Aid, CAFOD or Tearfund helps people in poverty. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One way is that Christian Aid provides emergency relief after disasters, such as food, clean water and shelter. It is supported by churches and Christian Aid Week. In Matthew 25:35 Jesus says 'I was hungry and you gave me something to eat'. This means Christians believe helping people in need is serving Jesus. Another way is that Christian Aid supports long-term projects and campaigns for fairer trade and action on climate change. This means it tackles the causes of poverty. Proverbs 19:17 says 'whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD', so Christians believe God rewards those who help.
points: Emergency aid: food, water, shelter
Long-term development projects
Campaigning for justice, trade, climate
Sources: Matthew 25:35-40, Mark 10:21, Proverbs 19:17, James 2:17
Details: Christian Aid 1945, CAFOD 1962, Tearfund 1968

exam.q: 'Private worship is more important than public worship for Christians.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Jesus taught Christians to pray privately: 'go into your room, close the door and pray' (Matthew 6:6).
Private worship can be done anywhere at any time and builds a personal relationship with God.
Public worship can be just routine or for show, whereas private worship is sincere.
against: Christians are called to be one body and worship together (1 Corinthians 12:27; Hebrews 10:25).
Public worship includes the sacraments, which cannot be done alone, and teaching from the Bible and sermons.
Worship together strengthens faith and gives community support.
exam.conclusion: Both are needed, but public worship is more important because the sacraments and the community are essential to being a Christian.
exam.model:
Some Christians agree that private worship is more important. Jesus taught that people should pray in private, saying 'go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father' (Matthew 6:6). Private worship allows a personal, honest relationship with God, anywhere and at any time, through prayer, Bible reading or using aids such as a rosary. Some Christians say public worship can become routine or be done to impress others, whereas private worship is sincere. This is a good argument because a relationship with God needs personal faith, and many Christians cannot attend church every day. However, it does not mean public worship is unimportant.

Other Christians argue that public worship is more important. Christians believe they belong to one body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:27) and are meant to worship together. The sacraments, such as baptism and Holy Communion, cannot be done alone, and Catholics believe the Mass is the most important act of worship. Public worship also teaches through the Bible and sermons, gives support, and unites Christians across the world. This argument is strong because it stresses the community nature of Christianity, and Jesus himself worshipped in the synagogue.

The Bible also says Christians should not give up meeting together (Hebrews 10:25), which supports gathering for worship.

In conclusion, I think public worship is more important because it includes the sacraments and community, which are central to Christianity. However, private worship is essential to make faith personal, and the two work best together. Most Christians would say they should not be set against each other, so the statement is only partly true.

exam.q: 'Infant baptism is better than believers' baptism.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Catholics believe it removes original sin, so babies should be baptised as soon as possible.
It welcomes the child into the Church and God's family, and parents and godparents promise to raise the child in the faith.
Jesus welcomed children (Mark 10:14) and the New Testament mentions whole households being baptised (Acts 16:33).
against: Faith should be a personal decision; babies cannot choose, so baptism has no meaning for them.
The New Testament examples, like Acts 2:38, show people baptised after repenting and believing.
Believers' baptism by immersion shows dying and rising with Christ and a public commitment.
exam.conclusion: Believers' baptism is more meaningful as a personal choice, but infant baptism also expresses God's grace; the better form depends on denomination and theology.
exam.model:
Some Christians believe infant baptism is better. Catholics teach that it removes original sin, so it is sensible to baptise babies quickly. It welcomes the child into the Church, and parents and godparents promise to raise the child in the faith. Jesus said 'Let the little children come to me' (Mark 10:14), and the New Testament describes whole households being baptised (Acts 16:33). This argument is strong for Christians who believe baptism is God's gift of grace rather than a human decision. However, it depends on accepting original sin and may seem to ignore the child's own choice.

Other Christians, such as Baptists, argue that believers' baptism is better. They believe faith is a personal decision, and a baby cannot repent or believe. The New Testament pattern is to repent first, then be baptised (Acts 2:38). Being fully immersed symbolises dying to sin and rising to new life, and the testimony gives a public commitment. This argument is convincing because it makes baptism meaningful for the person, and avoids people being baptised without understanding. Its weakness is that it can seem to exclude children from God's family.

Many Anglican families see baptism as the start of a journey, which is completed when the child chooses faith at confirmation.

In conclusion, I think believers' baptism is more meaningful because it expresses personal faith, but infant baptism has great value as a sign of God's love and welcome, and many infant-baptised Christians later confirm their faith. Which is 'better' depends on beliefs about sin and grace, so both can be valid for different Christians.

exam.q: 'Holy Communion is the most important sacrament for Christians.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: It was started by Jesus at the Last Supper ('Do this in remembrance of me', Luke 22:19) and is repeated regularly.
Catholics believe Jesus is really present and Christians receive grace and strengthen their faith.
It unites the congregation and sends Christians out to serve others.
against: Baptism is the first sacrament, makes people Christians and is practised by almost all Christians (Matthew 28:19).
Some Christians (Quakers, Salvation Army) have no sacraments and say faith matters more than ritual.
Other sacraments such as marriage and reconciliation matter in key moments of life.
exam.conclusion: Holy Communion is probably the most important for regular worship, though baptism is the foundation; importance depends on denomination.
exam.model:
Many Christians agree with this statement. Holy Communion began with Jesus at the Last Supper, when he told his followers 'Do this in remembrance of me' (Luke 22:19), so Christians obey him each time they celebrate. Catholics believe the bread and wine become Jesus' body and blood, so receiving it brings grace. It is repeated regularly, strengthening faith, uniting the congregation and encouraging service to others. This argument is strong because it is central to worship and Christians do it often, whereas baptism happens once.

Others argue that baptism is more important, because it makes someone a Christian, and Jesus commanded it (Matthew 28:19). Without baptism, a person cannot take Communion in many churches. Other Christians say sacraments are less important than faith and a good life: Quakers and the Salvation Army have no sacraments. Catholics also say that marriage, confession and others are important at key moments of life. This argument is persuasive for those who see baptism as the starting point of the Christian journey. However, it undervalues the weekly life of worship.

Communion also shows the unity of Christians, because believers share one loaf and one cup (1 Corinthians 10:17), so it shapes how the whole Church understands itself and its mission.

In conclusion, I think Holy Communion is the most important for ongoing Christian life, because it is shared regularly and remembers Jesus' sacrifice, while baptism is the foundation. Importance depends on the denomination, but because Communion shapes worship each week, I find the statement largely convincing.

exam.q: 'The most important task for the Church today is to spread the gospel.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Jesus gave the Great Commission: 'go and make disciples of all nations' (Matthew 28:19).
Spreading the gospel helps people find salvation and eternal life (John 14:6).
The Church exists to share Jesus' message; the Holy Spirit empowered the first disciples for this (Acts 1:8).
against: Jesus also taught practical love: caring for the hungry and sick (Matthew 25:35-40; James 2:17), so social action may be just as important.
People may be turned off by pressure to convert; example may be better than preaching.
Many churches see worship, reconciliation and justice as equally central.
exam.conclusion: Spreading the gospel is central but should go hand in hand with practical love; the Church's task is both words and actions.
exam.model:
Many Christians agree with this statement. Jesus gave the Great Commission, telling his followers to 'go and make disciples of all nations' (Matthew 28:19). Jesus promised that the Holy Spirit would give them power to be his witnesses (Acts 1:8), and at Pentecost the Spirit gave the disciples courage to spread the message. Christians believe Jesus is the way to salvation (John 14:6), so sharing the gospel could help others reach eternal life. This is a strong argument because it follows Jesus' direct command, and without it the Church would not grow. Evangelical and Pentecostal Christians especially see it as the main task.

Other Christians argue that practical action is equally or more important. In Matthew 25:35-40 Jesus says that helping the hungry and sick is serving him, and James says faith without action is dead. Many churches run food banks, Street Pastors and charities such as CAFOD, showing God's love in action. Some argue that people are more likely to listen to Christians who help them, and that pressuring people to convert can put them off. This argument is convincing because it fits Jesus' own example of healing and feeding people alongside teaching. Also, churches have other tasks, such as worship and reconciliation.

Jesus himself both preached and healed, which suggests that the Church's mission includes words and deeds together.

In conclusion, I believe spreading the gospel is vital, but it is not the only task. The strongest view is that words and actions go together: Christians show God's love practically and share the message when people are open to it. So the statement is partly right but too narrow.

exam.q: 'The Church should do more to end world poverty.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Jesus taught that helping the poor is serving him (Matthew 25:35-40) and told a rich man to give to the poor (Mark 10:21).
Poverty still affects millions, and the Church is a worldwide body with money, volunteers and influence.
Christians should campaign about causes of poverty, such as unfair trade and debt, as well as give aid.
against: Churches already do a great deal through CAFOD, Christian Aid and Tearfund, and local food banks.
Governments and international organisations have more power and money to end poverty; the Church should focus on worship and evangelism.
Some Christians worry that campaigning for political change distracts from spiritual mission.
exam.conclusion: Christians have a duty to help the poor, and while they already do much, the scale of poverty means they should do more, especially in campaigning for justice.
exam.model:
Many Christians agree that the Church should do more. Jesus taught that helping the hungry and thirsty is serving him (Matthew 25:35-40) and told a rich man to sell his possessions and give to the poor (Mark 10:21). Millions still live in poverty because of debt, conflict, unfair trade and disasters. The worldwide Church has many members, money and influence, so it could do more through campaigning and giving. James 2:17 says faith without action is dead. This is a strong argument because it follows Jesus' teaching and the Church has the resources, but it is difficult to judge how much more is 'enough'.

Others argue that the Church already does much. Charities such as CAFOD, Christian Aid and Tearfund provide emergency aid, long-term projects and campaigns, and local churches run food banks. Governments and international organisations have far more money and power to end poverty, so the Church's main focus should be worship and spreading the gospel. Some Christians worry that heavy political campaigning distracts from the spiritual mission. This argument is convincing because the Church's resources are limited and it has already helped millions.

Jesus also warned in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16) that ignoring the poor has serious consequences, so Christians cannot be satisfied with what has already been done.

In conclusion, I think the Church should do more, especially in campaigning for justice on things like debt and fair trade, because charity alone treats the symptoms of poverty. However, the Church already does a great deal and cannot end poverty alone. Therefore, the statement is largely right, because Christians have a duty to keep acting while poverty remains.

exam.q: Explain two reasons why worship is important for Christians. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One reason is that worship is the way Christians praise and thank God for who he is and what he has done. They believe God created them and saved them through Jesus, so it is right to respond with praise. Psalm 95:6 says 'Oh come, let's worship and bow down. Let's kneel before Yahweh, our Maker.' This means many Christians kneel, sing hymns and pray in church each Sunday as a way of honouring God. A second reason is that worshipping together builds up the Christian community and strengthens faith. The first Christians met for 'the apostles' teaching and fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer' (Acts 2:42). This means Christians today meet regularly to encourage each other, hear the Bible explained and share Holy Communion, so that their faith stays strong when life is difficult.
points: To praise and thank God as creator and saviour (Psalm 95:6)
To build community and strengthen faith (Acts 2:42, Hebrews 10:25)
To hear and learn from the Bible (2 Timothy 3:16)
To meet God, who is present when believers gather (Matthew 18:20)
Private worship builds a personal relationship (Matthew 6:6)
Application: e.g. 'so Christians attend church each Sunday'

exam.q: Explain two reasons why the Lord's Prayer is important for Christians. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One reason is that it was taught by Jesus himself. When the disciples asked how to pray, Jesus said 'Pray like this' and gave them the words in Matthew 6:9-13. This means Christians see it as the perfect model for prayer, so it is said in almost every type of service, from the Catholic Mass to Baptist worship, and many Christians say it every day. A second reason is that it teaches Christians how to live, not just how to pray. The line 'Forgive us our sins as we forgive those who sin against us' (based on Matthew 6:12) reminds them that they cannot ask for God's forgiveness while refusing to forgive others. This means that saying the prayer challenges Christians to let go of grudges and to put relationships right.
points: Taught by Jesus as a model (Matthew 6:9-13; Luke 11:2-4)
Unites Christians of all denominations, who all use it
Teaches forgiveness (Matthew 6:12)
Teaches dependence on God for daily needs ('daily bread')
Teaches putting God's will and kingdom first
Application: used daily and in most services

exam.q: 'Set prayers are more useful for Christians than informal prayer.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
exam.model:
Some Christians would agree with this statement. The most important Christian prayer, the Lord's Prayer, is a set prayer given by Jesus himself, who said 'Pray like this' (Matthew 6:9). Set prayers unite Christians: Catholics, Anglicans and Methodists around the world say the same words, so they feel part of one worldwide Church. They also help when people do not know what to say, for example when someone is grieving or anxious, and they make sure that prayer includes praise, confession and prayer for others, not just requests. Catholics value prayers such as the Hail Mary and the rosary because they help the mind focus on God. This is a strong argument, because Jesus' own example gives set prayer the highest authority.

However, many Christians, especially Evangelicals and Pentecostals, would disagree. They argue that informal prayer, in a person's own words, is more personal and honest, like talking to a friend. Jesus warned against 'vain repetitions' (Matthew 6:7), suggesting that words repeated without thought are worthless. Informal prayer can respond to the exact situation, such as praying for a sick friend by name, and Paul's instruction to 'pray without ceasing' (1 Thessalonians 5:17) suggests prayer should be a natural part of the whole day rather than only fixed words. This argument is also strong, because a relationship with God depends on sincerity.

Yet even informal prayer can become careless, and set prayers can be said with deep feeling. The value of prayer seems to depend more on the attitude of the person than on the type of words.

In conclusion, I disagree with the statement. Set prayers are very useful for unity, structure and times of difficulty, but informal prayer allows a personal relationship that set words alone cannot give. Most Christians use both, for example the Lord's Prayer followed by their own prayers, and this balance seems the most useful.
for: Jesus gave a set prayer (Matthew 6:9-13), so it has the highest authority.
Set prayers unite Christians worldwide and link them to tradition.
They help when people cannot find words and give a balanced pattern (praise, confession, intercession).
against: Informal prayer is personal and sincere, like talking to a friend.
Jesus warned against 'vain repetitions' (Matthew 6:7).
It can respond to specific needs and fit into the whole day (1 Thessalonians 5:17).
The attitude of the person matters more than the type of words.
exam.conclusion: Both are useful in different ways; sincerity matters most, so a balance of set and informal prayer is best, and set prayer is not more useful overall.

exam.q: Explain two reasons why baptism is important for Christians. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One reason is that Jesus commanded it. Before his ascension he told the disciples to make disciples of all nations, 'baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' (Matthew 28:19). This means Christians see baptism as an act of obedience, so almost all churches baptise new members, whether as babies or as believers. A second reason is that baptism marks the start of a new life with Christ. Paul says that in baptism Christians are 'buried with him' so that they can 'walk in newness of life' (Romans 6:4). This means that, especially in believers' baptism by full immersion, going under the water shows dying to an old, sinful life and coming up shows rising to a new life as a follower of Jesus.
points: Jesus commanded it (Matthew 28:19) and was baptised himself (Mark 1:9-11)
Cleansing from sin, including original sin for Catholics (Acts 2:38)
New life with Christ: dying and rising (Romans 6:4)
Joining the Church, the family of God
Receiving the Holy Spirit and God's grace (John 3:5)
Application: infant or believers' baptism, testimony, godparents

exam.q: Explain two reasons why Holy Communion is important for Christians. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One reason is that Jesus commanded his followers to celebrate it. At the Last Supper he took bread and said 'This is my body which is given for you. Do this in memory of me' (Luke 22:19). This means Christians believe they are obeying Jesus when they share bread and wine, so for Catholics the Mass is the centre of Sunday worship and other churches hold Communion regularly. A second reason is that it unites Christians with each other and with Christ. Paul wrote that because there is one loaf, 'we, who are many, are one body' (1 Corinthians 10:17). This means that sharing Communion brings a congregation together as a family, and Catholics and Orthodox believe they truly receive Christ himself, which gives them grace and strength to serve others in the week ahead.
points: Jesus commanded it at the Last Supper (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24)
Remembers and proclaims Jesus' death (1 Corinthians 11:26)
Unites believers as one body (1 Corinthians 10:17)
Christ is really present: Catholic transubstantiation (John 6:53)
Gives grace and strength; encourages service and justice
Application: weekly Mass, monthly Communion, open table

exam.q: Explain two contrasting reasons why Christians might go on pilgrimage. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One reason is to seek healing. Many Catholics travel to Lourdes, where Bernadette saw visions of Mary in 1858, hoping for a cure or for strength to cope with illness. They bathe in the spring water and pray at the Grotto, trusting Jesus' invitation 'Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest' (Matthew 11:28). This means sick pilgrims and their carers go expecting God to bring physical or spiritual healing. A contrasting reason is to find peace and quiet in order to reflect. Pilgrims to the island of Iona join simple daily worship in the abbey and spend time walking and thinking about their lives. Psalm 46:10 says 'Be still, and know that I am God'. This means they step away from the noise of everyday life so they can listen to God and return home with a clearer sense of how to live.
points: Healing (Lourdes): Matthew 11:28
Quiet reflection and peace (Iona): Psalm 46:10
Forgiveness and making a fresh start
Strengthening faith by visiting places linked to Jesus or saints (Holy Land; Luke 2:41)
Meeting other Christians and helping the sick
Catechism 2691: pilgrimage as renewal in prayer and a picture of the journey to heaven

exam.q: 'Pilgrimage is not necessary for Christians today.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
exam.model:
Many Christians would agree with this statement. Christianity does not require pilgrimage, unlike Hajj in Islam. Christians believe God is everywhere, and Jesus said that God is worshipped 'in spirit and truth' (John 4:24), not only in special places. Quakers and many Protestants say no place is holier than another, so a person can be as close to God in their bedroom as at Lourdes. Pilgrimages can also be expensive and difficult for poorer or sick people, and the money might be better given to the poor, as Jesus told the rich man to do (Mark 10:21). This argument is strong because it fits the Christian belief that salvation comes from faith in Jesus, not from visiting places.

However, other Christians argue that, while pilgrimage is not compulsory, it can be extremely valuable. The Catechism of the Catholic Church describes pilgrimages as 'special occasions for renewal in prayer' and a picture of life's journey towards heaven. Jesus' family went to Jerusalem every year at Passover (Luke 2:41), so pilgrimage has deep roots. Many sick pilgrims at Lourdes describe spiritual healing and new hope, even when they are not physically cured, and volunteers who care for them grow in compassion. On Iona, people find peace and time to reflect away from busy modern life, which may be harder to find at home today than in the past. This argument is strong because it is based on the real experience of millions of Christians.

The word 'necessary' is important. Pilgrimage is not necessary for salvation, but something can be unnecessary and still very helpful.

In conclusion, I agree with the statement in a strict sense: Christians do not need pilgrimage to be saved or to know God. However, I think it would be wrong to dismiss it, because for many people it deepens faith in a way that everyday life cannot, especially in today's busy world.
for: Christianity does not require pilgrimage; God is everywhere (John 4:24).
Quakers and many Protestants say no place is holier than another.
It can be expensive; the money could help the poor (Mark 10:21).
Salvation is through faith in Jesus, not visiting places.
against: Catechism 2691: pilgrimage renews prayer and pictures the journey to heaven.
Jesus' family made pilgrimage (Luke 2:41).
Lourdes offers healing and hope; Iona offers peace and reflection in a busy world.
Pilgrims and volunteers grow in faith and compassion.
exam.conclusion: Pilgrimage is not necessary for salvation, but it is valuable and can deepen faith, so 'not necessary' should not mean 'not important'.

exam.q: Explain two reasons why Christmas is important for Christians in Great Britain today. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One reason is that Christmas celebrates the incarnation, when God became human in Jesus. John's Gospel says 'The Word became flesh, and lived among us' (John 1:14). This means that Christians in Britain go to Midnight Mass or carol services to thank God for coming to share human life, and they use lights and candles because Jesus is the light of the world. A second reason is that Christmas is a chance to show God's love to others and to share their faith in a society where many people celebrate without the religious meaning. The angels announced 'good news of great joy which will be to all the people' (Luke 2:10). This means many British churches run Christmas lunches for lonely or homeless people, support charity appeals and invite the wider community to nativity and Christingle services, which may be the only time some people visit a church.
points: Celebrates the incarnation (John 1:14; Luke 2:11)
Good news for all, so outreach and mission at carol services (Luke 2:10)
Giving gifts and charity, like the wise men (Matthew 2:11)
Jesus as light of the world: candles, Christingle (John 8:12)
In Britain: public holiday, many attend church only at Christmas, concern about commercialisation
Application: Midnight Mass, homeless meals, charity appeals

exam.q: 'Christmas has lost its religious meaning in Great Britain today.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
exam.model:
There are strong reasons to agree with this statement. In the 2021 census fewer than half of people in England and Wales described themselves as Christian, yet almost everyone celebrates Christmas. For many families it is mainly about presents, food, decorations and time off work. Shops begin selling Christmas goods weeks before Advent, and Father Christmas is more visible than the baby Jesus in adverts and on television. Many Christians worry that the festival has become commercial, with people spending money they cannot afford, which goes against Jesus' warnings about wealth. This argument is strong because it describes what many people actually experience.

However, there are also good reasons to disagree. For Christians, Christmas still celebrates the incarnation, the belief that 'the Word became flesh, and lived among us' (John 1:14). Churches are often fuller at Christmas than at any other time, with carol services, Midnight Mass, nativity plays and Christingle services drawing people who rarely attend. Many traditions that look secular still carry Christian meanings: gifts recall the wise men (Matthew 2:11) and lights recall Jesus as the light of the world. Christmas is a public holiday because of Britain's Christian heritage, and the King's Christmas broadcast often speaks about the Christian story. Churches also use the season to help others, for example by providing meals for homeless people, which reflects Jesus' teaching to care for the poor. This argument is strong because it shows that the religious meaning is still clearly present for millions.

Perhaps the truth is that Christmas has two meanings in Britain today, a cultural one and a religious one, existing side by side.

In conclusion, I disagree with the statement. The religious meaning has been weakened for many people and is often hidden by commercialism, but it has not been lost. For Christians, and for many others who attend a service or support charity at Christmas, the celebration of Jesus' birth remains at its heart.
for: Fewer than half in England and Wales called themselves Christian in 2021, yet nearly all celebrate Christmas.
Commercialism: shopping, Father Christmas and adverts dominate.
Spending and excess go against Jesus' teaching about wealth.
against: Christians still celebrate the incarnation (John 1:14); churches are fullest at Christmas.
Traditions carry religious meaning: gifts (Matthew 2:11), lights (John 8:12).
Public holiday and King's broadcast reflect Christian heritage.
Churches use Christmas for charity and outreach.
exam.conclusion: The religious meaning is weakened for many but not lost: cultural and religious Christmas exist side by side.

exam.q: Explain two different ways in which the Church helps people in the local community. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is by running food banks. Many churches host Trussell food banks, where volunteers give emergency food parcels to people referred by doctors or social workers, often with a hot drink and someone to listen. A different way is by supporting young people. Churches run youth clubs and toddler groups in their halls, giving children a safe place to meet, play and learn, and giving parents support and friendship.
points: Food banks: emergency food parcels, volunteers, Trussell Trust
Street Pastors: caring for people in town centres at night
Youth clubs and toddler groups
Lunch clubs and coffee mornings for lonely or elderly people
Debt advice, night shelters, warm spaces
Services for local events and a quiet place to pray

exam.q: 'Helping people in the local community is more important for the Church than worship.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
exam.model:
Some Christians would agree with this statement. Jesus taught that people will be judged on how they treated the hungry, the stranger and the sick: 'I was hungry, and you gave me food to eat' (Matthew 25:35). James says faith without works is dead (James 2:17), and 1 John 3:17 asks how God's love can be in someone who ignores a person in need. In Britain today millions of food parcels are given out each year, many through church food banks, and Street Pastors care for vulnerable people at night. This practical love shows the community what Christianity means far more clearly than services that only churchgoers attend. This is a strong argument because it is grounded directly in Jesus' teaching about judgement.

Other Christians disagree. They argue that worship comes first because the greatest commandment is to love God, and only then to love your neighbour (Mark 12:29-31). Worship, especially Holy Communion, is where Christians receive the strength and grace to serve; without it, community work could become just another charity. Jesus himself went away to pray before serving others (Mark 1:35). The first Christians devoted themselves to teaching, fellowship, breaking bread and prayer (Acts 2:42), and their care for each other grew out of that worship. This argument is strong because it explains where the motivation for service comes from.

Many Christians say the two cannot be separated. Worship that ignores the poor is empty (the prophet Amos condemned this), but service without prayer loses its Christian heart. Many churches link them directly, for example by collecting food during services for the local food bank.

In conclusion, I disagree that helping the community is more important. Both are essential, but worship is the root and service is the fruit. A church that only served would lose its source of strength, while a church that only worshipped would fail to follow Jesus.
for: Sheep and goats (Matthew 25:35-40): judged on care for the needy.
Faith without works is dead (James 2:17); 1 John 3:17.
Food banks and Street Pastors show Christian love to the whole community.
against: The first commandment is to love God (Mark 12:29-31); worship comes first.
Worship and Communion give the strength and grace to serve.
Jesus prayed before serving (Mark 1:35); the early Church's care grew from worship (Acts 2:42).
The two belong together: service is the fruit of worship.
exam.conclusion: Both are essential and linked; worship is the root and service the fruit, so community work is not more important.

exam.q: Explain two different ways in which Street Pastors help people. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is by giving practical help to people who are vulnerable at night. Street Pastors hand out water, flip-flops and foil blankets, and make sure people who are very drunk or alone get home safely, which can prevent injuries and crime. A different way is by offering a listening ear. They stop and talk with anyone who wants to chat, including people who are upset or lonely, and they will pray with someone if asked, showing that someone cares about them without judging.
points: Practical help: water, flip-flops, blankets
Safety: helping vulnerable people get home, reducing violence
Listening and emotional support
Praying with people if asked
Working with police, councils and door staff to calm situations
Picking up glass bottles to prevent injuries

exam.q: 'Street Pastors are the best example of Christians helping their local community.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
exam.model:
Some people would agree with this statement. Street Pastors go out to where people are, late at night in town centres, rather than waiting for them to come to church. They care for people who are drunk, lost or in danger, often people who would never go near a church, which matches the parable of the Good Samaritan, where help is given to a stranger lying by the road (Luke 10:25-37). They work closely with police and councils, who often welcome their presence. They also help without judging, following Jesus' words 'Don't judge, so that you won't be judged' (Matthew 7:1). This argument is strong because Street Pastors show Christian love in a very visible and costly way, giving up their weekend nights.

However, there are good arguments for other examples. Food banks probably help far more people: Trussell food banks alone gave out around 2.6 million emergency parcels in 2025. Hunger is a basic need, and Jesus said 'I was hungry, and you gave me food' (Matthew 25:35). Food bank volunteers also offer advice that helps people out of crisis. Other churches run lunch clubs for lonely elderly people or youth clubs that support young people every week, building long-term relationships rather than brief contact on a single night. These may change lives more deeply. It could also be argued that worship and prayer are the Church's most important gift to a community.

Which is 'best' depends on what is being measured: numbers helped, depth of support, or reaching people no one else reaches.

In conclusion, I disagree that Street Pastors are clearly the best example. They are an outstanding way of reaching people who are vulnerable and far from church, but food banks meet a more basic need for many more people. The strongest Christian response is a range of projects, all expressing 'love your neighbour as yourself' (Mark 12:31).
for: They go to where people are and reach those far from church.
They follow the Good Samaritan (Luke 10) and do not judge (Matthew 7:1).
Visible, costly service that helps keep people safe.
against: Food banks help far more people with a basic need (Matthew 25:35); about 2.6 million Trussell parcels in 2025.
Weekly youth clubs and lunch clubs build long-term relationships.
Some say worship and prayer are the Church's greatest gift.
exam.conclusion: Street Pastors are an excellent example but not clearly the best; food banks meet a more basic need for more people, and a range of projects best expresses love of neighbour.

exam.q: Explain two different ways in which Christians carry out evangelism. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is through courses such as Alpha. Churches invite people to a meal, a short talk about Jesus and an open discussion where any question can be asked, so people can explore Christianity in a relaxed setting. A different way is through personal witness. Individual Christians share their own story of faith with friends and colleagues, or simply live in a loving way that makes others curious, following 1 Peter 3:15 to be ready to explain their hope.
points: Alpha and similar courses
Personal witness and testimony
Preaching, street evangelism and outreach events
Missionaries working abroad
Social media, TV, radio and online services
Living by example and serving others

exam.q: Explain two different methods Christians use to bring about Church growth. (4 marks)
exam.model: One method is starting new forms of church that reach people who would not go to a traditional service. For example, Messy Church invites families to crafts, a short Bible story and a meal, and café churches meet in relaxed settings, so people can explore faith without feeling out of place. A different method is using the media. Churches stream services online, post short videos on social media and run podcasts, which can reach young people and those who are housebound far beyond the church building.
points: Fresh Expressions such as Messy Church and café church
Church planting: starting new congregations
Courses such as Alpha
Social media, online services, TV and radio
Personal invitation and testimony
Practical service that attracts people (food banks, youth work)

exam.q: Explain two reasons why Christians work to bring about Church growth. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One reason is that Jesus commanded it. Before his ascension he told his followers to 'make disciples of all nations' (Matthew 28:19). This means Christians see helping the Church grow as obedience to Jesus, so they invite friends to church, support Alpha courses and fund missionaries. A second reason is that they believe the gospel brings salvation, so they want as many people as possible to hear it. Jesus said 'I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me' (John 14:6). This means Christians believe that by helping the Church grow they are offering others the chance of forgiveness and eternal life with God, which they see as the greatest gift they can share.
points: The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19-20)
Salvation through Jesus (John 14:6)
The early Church grew through the Spirit (Acts 2:41, 2:47)
A bigger Church can do more good in the community
To keep the faith alive in places where it is declining
Growth in faith (discipleship), not only numbers

exam.q: 'Church growth is the most important task for Christians today.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
exam.model:
Many Christians, especially Evangelicals and Pentecostals, would agree with this statement. Jesus' last command before his ascension was the Great Commission: 'Go and make disciples of all nations' (Matthew 28:19). Christians believe that Jesus is 'the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6), so helping people come to faith is the most loving thing they can do, because it offers them eternal life. In Britain the 2021 census showed that fewer than half of people called themselves Christian for the first time, so some argue that without growth the Church could disappear from many communities. A growing Church also has more people and money to serve the poor. This argument is strong, because if Christians believe the gospel is true, sharing it must be a high priority.

However, other Christians argue that other tasks are as important or more important. Jesus said the greatest commandments are to love God and love your neighbour (Mark 12:29-31), not to increase numbers. The parable of the sheep and the goats says people will be judged on caring for the hungry, sick and imprisoned (Matthew 25), so work such as food banks, Street Pastors and supporting persecuted Christians may matter more. Some also warn that focusing on numbers can lead to pressuring people, which disrespects their freedom and other faiths. Paul wrote 'I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase' (1 Corinthians 3:6), suggesting growth is God's work, while Christians' task is to be faithful. This argument is strong because it reflects Jesus' own priorities.

The two sides can be connected: churches that serve their communities in love often grow as a result, as in Acts 2:47, where the early Christians had 'favour with all the people'.

In conclusion, I disagree that Church growth is the single most important task. Love of God and neighbour comes first, and growth is best seen as a result of faithful worship and service rather than a goal pursued for its own sake.
for: The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19) was Jesus' final command.
Salvation through Jesus (John 14:6): sharing faith is the most loving act.
Decline in Britain (2021 census) threatens the Church's future; a larger Church can serve more.
against: The greatest commandments are love of God and neighbour (Mark 12:29-31).
Judgement is on care for the needy (Matthew 25).
Focusing on numbers can pressure people; growth is God's work (1 Corinthians 3:6).
Service often leads to growth anyway (Acts 2:47).
exam.conclusion: Love of God and neighbour comes first; growth is a fruit of faithful worship and service rather than the most important task in itself.

exam.q: Explain two different ways in which Christians work for reconciliation. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is through organised projects that bring divided communities together. The Corrymeela Community in Northern Ireland invites Catholics, Protestants and people of all backgrounds to meet, talk and build trust after years of violence. A different way is through personal forgiveness. A Christian who has been hurt by someone may choose to forgive and rebuild the friendship, and Catholics may receive the sacrament of reconciliation to restore their relationship with God.
points: Community projects: Corrymeela, Coventry's Community of the Cross of Nails
National processes: Desmond Tutu and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission
Personal forgiveness and restoring friendships
The Catholic sacrament of reconciliation
Ecumenism: churches working for unity (World Council of Churches)
Prayer for peace, such as the Coventry Litany of Reconciliation

exam.q: 'Working for reconciliation is the most important role of the worldwide Church.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
exam.model:
Some Christians would agree with this statement. They believe the heart of the gospel is reconciliation: 'God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself' (2 Corinthians 5:19), and Paul says God has given Christians 'the ministry of reconciliation' (2 Corinthians 5:18). Jesus said 'Blessed are the peacemakers' (Matthew 5:9) and even told people to be reconciled with others before offering worship (Matthew 5:23-24). History shows the Church doing this powerfully: Desmond Tutu helped South Africa move on from apartheid through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, the Corrymeela Community has brought Catholics and Protestants together in Northern Ireland, and after Coventry Cathedral was bombed in 1940 its leaders chose 'Father Forgive' rather than revenge. In a world with many conflicts, this role is something few other organisations can offer. This argument is strong because it reflects what Christians believe God himself has done.

However, other Christians would argue that other roles are equally or more important. Millions of people live in extreme poverty, and Jesus said that people will be judged on whether they fed the hungry and cared for the sick (Matthew 25:35-40), so the work of CAFOD, Christian Aid and Tearfund could be seen as more urgent. Others argue that supporting persecuted Christians, of whom Open Doors estimated more than 388 million faced high levels of persecution in 2026, is the worldwide Church's first duty to its own members (1 Corinthians 12:26). Evangelicals may say that spreading the gospel matters most, because of the Great Commission.

These roles overlap: poverty and persecution often follow from conflict, so reconciliation can help to tackle them, and sharing the gospel is itself a message of reconciliation with God.

In conclusion, I think reconciliation is one of the most important roles, because it lies at the centre of Christian belief about what Jesus did. However, calling it 'the most important' is too strong, since Jesus also commanded care for the poor and the spreading of the gospel, and the worldwide Church needs to do all three.
for: Reconciliation is at the heart of the gospel (2 Corinthians 5:18-19).
Jesus blessed peacemakers (Matthew 5:9) and put reconciliation before worship (Matthew 5:23-24).
Powerful examples: Tutu, Corrymeela, Coventry's 'Father Forgive'.
against: Fighting poverty is urgent: Matthew 25:35-40; CAFOD, Christian Aid, Tearfund.
Supporting persecuted believers (Open Doors 2026: over 388 million; 1 Corinthians 12:26).
Evangelicals may see the Great Commission as the first task.
The roles overlap, so ranking them is difficult.
exam.conclusion: Reconciliation is central to Christian belief, but the worldwide Church is also called to fight poverty and share the gospel, so it is one of the most important roles rather than the single most important.

exam.q: Explain two different ways in which Christians respond to persecution. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is by giving practical help. Christians in Britain give money to charities such as Open Doors, which provides Bibles, training and emergency aid to believers in countries where they are persecuted. A different way is through forgiveness and prayer. Following Jesus' command to 'pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you', many persecuted Christians refuse to take revenge and pray for their attackers, and churches worldwide hold prayer events for them.
points: Practical aid through Open Doors, Barnabas Aid, Release International
Campaigning and lobbying governments (CSW)
Prayer for persecuted Christians
Forgiving persecutors and refusing violence (Matthew 5:44)
Writing letters to prisoners (Hebrews 13:3)
Standing firm in faith despite danger

exam.q: 'Christians should always forgive those who persecute them.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
exam.model:
Many Christians would agree with this statement. Jesus taught 'love your enemies... and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you' (Matthew 5:44), and he practised this himself on the cross, praying 'Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing' (Luke 23:34). Stephen, the first Christian martyr, prayed for those stoning him (Acts 7:60). In the Lord's Prayer Christians ask God to forgive them as they forgive others, which suggests that refusing to forgive blocks their own relationship with God. There are modern examples of persecuted Christians forgiving their attackers publicly, which has made a powerful impression on others. This argument is strong because it comes directly from Jesus' words and example.

However, some Christians argue that 'always' is too strong. Forgiveness does not mean ignoring injustice. God is just, and the Bible calls believers to 'seek justice' and 'relieve the oppressed' (Isaiah 1:17). Organisations like Christian Solidarity Worldwide campaign for persecutors to be held to account and for laws to change. Some victims may need time to forgive, and forcing them to forgive quickly could add to their pain. Others argue that forgiveness depends on the wrongdoer being sorry, and that a persecutor who continues to harm people should first stop. This argument has weight because forgiveness without justice could seem to accept evil.

Many Christians would say that forgiveness and justice can go together: a person can forgive in their heart, refusing hatred and revenge, while still wanting the persecution to end and the guilty to face the truth. Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission tried to combine truth-telling with forgiveness.

In conclusion, I agree that Christians should aim to forgive persecutors, because Jesus' teaching and example are very clear. However, forgiveness does not mean staying silent, and it can be a long process, so 'always' should mean always aiming to forgive, while still working for justice.
for: Jesus commanded love and prayer for persecutors (Matthew 5:44).
Jesus forgave from the cross (Luke 23:34); Stephen did too (Acts 7:60).
The Lord's Prayer links being forgiven with forgiving others.
against: God is just; Christians must 'seek justice' (Isaiah 1:17); CSW campaigns for accountability.
Victims may need time; forced forgiveness can add to pain.
Some say forgiveness needs repentance first.
Forgiveness and justice can go together (Truth and Reconciliation Commission).
exam.conclusion: Christians should always aim to forgive, as Jesus did, but forgiveness is a process and does not mean giving up on justice.

exam.q: Explain two different ways in which CAFOD, Christian Aid or Tearfund helps people in poverty. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is emergency aid. When an earthquake, flood or war strikes, Christian Aid works with local partners to provide food, clean water, shelter and medical care straight away, saving lives in the first days of a crisis. A different way is long-term development. Christian Aid supports projects such as training farmers to grow crops that can survive drought, so families can earn a living and feed themselves for years to come instead of relying on aid.
points: Emergency aid: food, water, shelter, medicine after disasters
Long-term development: wells, farming, education, healthcare
Campaigning: fair trade, debt, tax justice, climate change
Working through local partners and churches (Tearfund)
Fundraising and education in UK churches and schools (Christian Aid Week, Family Fast Day)
